items.title: The Theoretical Evolution, Knowledge Structure, and Digital-Intelligent Turn of the Production-Oriented Approach: A Study Based on CNKI Literature
items.abstract: Based on the studies on the Production-Oriented Approach (POA) included in the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and combining bibliometrics with close reading, this paper examines the research characteristics, conceptual evolution, and digital-intelligent turn of this theory. The findings show that POA research has moved from rapid growth into a stage of stable deepening, with core authors and institutions becoming concentrated, and research themes expanding from college English to teaching Chinese to speakers of other languages, less commonly taught languages, textbook development, and intelligent teaching. Centered on the problem of 'separating learning from use,' the theory has refined its teaching principles, hypotheses, and procedures, forming a four-dimensional teaching framework that links learning, use, and assessment in a closed loop, together with a unit-nested teaching procedure. Generative artificial intelligence can empower teaching, yet existing studies are mostly short-cycle, single-course, and small-sample practices. Future research should carry out cross-language and cross-stage long-cycle comparisons, and build a human-machine collaborative assessment system based on classroom production, so as to address problems such as data bias, the weakening of teachers' subjectivity, and technology dependence.

items.title: The waiting room safety net: An evolutionary concept analysis of patient safety in the emergency department waiting room
items.abstract: Background: Emergency departments represent a critical point of access to healthcare in Canada, yet escalating pressures from overcrowding are putting patients at increased risk of preventable harm due to increased waiting times. Emergency department waiting rooms are evolving from passive holding spaces to extensions of the clinical care environment however, these spaces are not optimized to facilitate patient safety (Zamani, 2019), putting vulnerable individuals waiting for care at risk of deterioration and adverse outcomes. Waiting room safety netting emerges as a nascent, fragmented idea in the literature yet lacks the specificity and contextual grounding to be operationalized to quality improvement initiatives and patient safety planning. This study aimed to explicate the concept of an ED Waiting Room Safety Net utilizing Rodger’s evolutionary concept analysis to identify the antecedents, attributes and consequences of this construct to inform a systems-oriented, contextually adaptable model for patient safety in emergency care. Methods: Rodger’s evolutionary concept analysis was chosen as the method focuses on concepts emerging through praxis rather than discrete conceptualization acknowledging that meaning arises through practice. Concept analysis occurs through six phases: identifying the concept and related terms, selecting the context and sample for data collection, gathering relevant data, analyzing for attributes, antecedents, and consequences, identifying an exemplar, and determining implications for future development. Results: 52 studies were identified through PubMed using combinations of surrogate terms, 18 scholarly works between 2017 and 2025, were selected and synthesized to derive the antecedents, attributes and consequences of a waiting room safety net. The Waiting Room Safety Net can be defined as: A proactive, responsive, and structured patient safety construct that involves optimizing human factors, technology, organizational processes, and the physical environment such that they interact to facilitate protective oversight of individuals in the emergency department waiting room and enable the avoidance of preventable harm while making the waiting experience more amenable to patients. The synthesis of 18 studies revealed eight thematic attributes which were consolidated into a conceptual model. Implications and lessons learned: A waiting room safety net emphasizes the balanced integration of human oversight, technological innovation and adaptive, aligned organizational processes. Fundamental processes include structured surveillance, clear communication, accountability and escalation pathways. This model offers a systems-thinking informed scaffold for waiting room patient safety and quality improvement initiatives.

items.title: Theorising Dementia as a Risk Classification: Sociotechnical Imaginaries of Safety and Order in Acute Hospital Care of People Living with Dementia
items.abstract: People living with dementia are one of the populations most at risk of restrictive intervention during an acute hospital admission. These restrictive interventions are typically justified by staff concerns about patient safety and as a means of mitigating against falls, itself a key metric of quality care in acute settings. Drawing on Jasanoff and Kim’s concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, this paper explores how healthcare professionals imagine risk and safety, and how these imaginaries contour the use of restrictive practice. Data collection comprised 225 days of ethnographic observation and 1168 in situ interviews with patients, families, and ward staff at (n = 6) NHS Trusts working in (n = 3) dyads for acute and mental health care across England. Data were analysed thematically using NVivo. Findings were grouped into three major themes: institutional cultures, institutional anxiety, and atrocity stories. The study reveals tensions between ways in which people living with dementia respond to admissions and the institutional imaginaries of a safe, risk-free ward, alongside expectations of “good patienthood.” It argues that these imaginaries produce dementia as a risk classification, where bed or bedside-bound patients who do not demand staff attention inform the routine use of restrictive practices. These interventions, however, often result in distress and feelings of imprisonment among people living with dementia, which in turn prompts further tightening of restraints on this vulnerable population.

items.title: TOWARDS PRECISION-CONTROLLED PARTONIC STRUCTURES FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES
items.abstract: The internal structure of hadrons is governed by nonperturbative Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and is being probed with increasing precision by modern high-energy experiments. This dissertation presents first-principles calculations of partonic observables using lattice QCD together with effective field theory methods, with controlled systematic uncertainties, advancing from collinear structure to transverse-momentum-dependent distributions (TMDs) that encode the three-dimensional partonic structure of hadrons. Within the large momentum effective theory (LaMET) framework, this work presents state-of-the-art calculations of pion distribution amplitudes and systematic studies of nucleon parton distributions, with control of renormalization, excited-state contamination, Fourier-transform systematics, and power corrections. A Coulomb-gauge formulation of quasi-distributions is implemented to simplify ultraviolet structure by avoiding Wilson-line related linear divergences. Systematic effects associated with Gribov copies are quantified and found to be negligible at current statistical precision, supporting the effectiveness of this approach. Building on these developments, this dissertation reports first-principles lattice determinations of key TMD quantities, including nucleon TMD parton distributions, the Collins-Soper kernel, the intrinsic soft function, and pion TMD observables. These results provide nonperturbative inputs directly relevant to global QCD analyses and to the precision hadron-structure program at current and future facilities, including the Electron-Ion Collider. In parallel, this dissertation explores machine-learning acceleration of lattice gauge simulations through neural field transformations embedded in Hybrid Monte Carlo. In two-dimensional U(1) tests, the method significantly reduces autocorrelation and improves performance toward finer lattice spacing. Such gains support precision-controlled partonic calculations by enabling finer lattices and larger hadron boosts, thereby reducing LaMET power corrections and improving control of discretization effects. The dissertation also outlines emerging directions using AI agents and foundation models to advance lattice data-analysis workflows under physics-based constraints.
topics: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies

items.title: TRIDENT-Seq: Profile-Matched Prefix-Future Contrast for Label-Efficient Payment Risk Modeling
items.abstract: Ant International accumulates large volumes of transaction history across users and payment businesses. Confirmed fraud and chargeback outcomes, by contrast, are scarce, delayed, and specific to each business. A single encoder pretrained on unlabeled histories could serve all businesses, but only if pretraining captures the behavior that separates risk. Coarse activity differences can make contrastive pretraining on transaction logs too easy: transaction volume, amount, and timing can distinguish a history's continuation from arbitrary candidates without modeling how payment resources are used. We present TRIDENT-Seq, a transaction foundation model trained with Prefix-Future Contrast (PFC). PFC matches each prefix to a summary of its subsequent behavior among candidates with similar activity profiles; activity prediction and dispersion regularization act on the encoder output. Across three production payment businesses, the pretrained encoder improves average precision (AP) and recall at a 0.5% intervention budget over architecture-matched scratch training in all six business-budget settings. With a fixed validation set, it exceeds full-label scratch training in mean AP and recall using 10% of the training labels on Wallet and 25% on Shopping and SME. Pretraining only on another business's histories still helps. Replacing profile-matched candidates with random ones cuts recall from 24.62% to 5.64%. In Ant International's deployment evaluation, recorded amount-based chargeback and overall loss rates are 37.7% and 37.9% lower than those of the previous XGBoost-based system under the same intervention budget.

items.title: Trust as a Mediating Factor in Enhancing Investors' Intention to Use Robo-Advising
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has developed rapidly in recent years. Beyond its specialized domains, it has also been applied to an increasing range of other fields. Prior research suggests that traditional financial decisions are typically reached through investors' own judgment, and that such judgment is readily subject to interference from human factors and other considerations, which compromises the accuracy of the resulting decisions. In response, many developers have introduced AI into the financial industry and integrated it with investment services, giving rise to a novel form of advisory known as robo-advising, or intelligent investment advisory. Robo-advising not only breaks with the conventional human-based advisory model through AI technologies, but also helps investors make more effective decisions, thereby reducing potential losses. Existing studies have proposed that the perceived usefulness of robo-advisory technology affects users' attitude and usage intention, and that information transparency likewise affects users' attitude and usage intention, with attitude positively related to usage intention. However, relatively few studies have examined trust as a mediating mechanism through which these factors shape investors' intention to use robo-advisory. Accordingly, this study employs correlation analysis, regression analysis, and structural equation modeling to analyze the data collected from a questionnaire survey and to test the proposed hypotheses. The findings indicate that the perceived usefulness and information transparency of robo-advising are capable of establishing investor trust, and that such trust can alter investors' attitude toward robo-advising, thereby enhancing their usage intention. In addition, this study aims to offer more effective recommendations for robo-advisory technology and to support the continued development of robo-advisory investment services.

items.title: Trust at the Interface: Consumer Trust, Transparency and Persuasion Knowledge in AI-Mediated Marketing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now selects, personalises, writes and voices marketing communications, placing an algorithmic agent at the interface between firms and consumers. Yet the evidence on how consumers respond is fragmented across three largely separate literatures — studies of AI disclosure, of personalisation and privacy, and of algorithm appreciation and aversion — which imply conflicting managerial defaults. This paper integrates these literatures through a single interpretive mechanism drawn from the Persuasion Knowledge Model: persuasion-knowledge activation. We argue that interface design choices — whether AI involvement is disclosed, whether data collection is overt or covert, how humanlike the agent appears, and how the task is framed — do not act on trust directly. They act by changing what consumers infer about the persuader's goals and competence, an inference process in which privacy calculus, uniqueness neglect and identity threat also operate. The resulting Trust at the Interface framework links interface signals to consumer appraisals, to trust attributions directed separately at the AI system and at the firm, and to behaviour, and adds a failure-and-repair loop explaining asymmetric blame and recovery after AI errors. Seven formal propositions specify the framework's testable claims, with implications for interface design, consumer protection and future research.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

items.title: Trust Calibration in Older Adults’ Human–Robot Interaction: A Dual-Path Model of Cognitive and Emotional Trust
items.abstract: As service robots are increasingly deployed in eldercare settings, trust calibration following robot errors has become a core issue affecting the effectiveness of human-robot collaboration. Focusing on older adult users, this study systematically investigates the joint influence mechanism of error situations and explanation strategies on trust calibration through a 2 (error severity: high vs. low) × 2 (transparency: high vs. low) mixed-design experiment, and further tests a cognitive–emotional dual-path model of trust calibration. Using video-based scenario simulation combined with scale-based measurement, the study was conducted with 80 older adults. Results show that high-severity errors significantly undermine both cognitive trust and emotional trust, with a more pronounced detrimental effect on cognitive trust. Transparency interventions primarily facilitate trust repair through the emotional trust pathway, with no significant direct effect on cognitive trust. The study further reveals that transparency is more effective in repairing trust under low-severity error conditions, and that individuals' technology anxiety significantly attenuates the repair efficacy of transparency on the cognitive pathway. These findings not only provide preliminary empirical evidence for a dual-path dissociation pattern in older adults' trust repair—characterized by emotional priority and cognitive lag—but also offer an important empirical basis and design directions for developing age-appropriate service robots with context-awareness, emotional interaction, and personalized adaptation capabilities.

items.title: Uncovering Why LLMs Fail: From Internal Mechanisms to Adversarial Reasoning Trajectories
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are usually evaluated by final-output correctness or safety, yet an endpoint label does not reveal how a failure develops throughout the reasoning process. We therefore ask whether ordinary reasoning failures and adversarially induced failures can be characterized using the same internal coordinates. Towards this end, we in this paper study a white-box diagnostic framework CauTrace to disclose the root-cause of why LLM fails from three fundamental inspections: Functional States, Propagation of Representation, Temporal-State Coordination and Reasoning Trajectory. First, seven functional states are creatively defined to represent the support and constraint processing in LLMs. Second, the propagation of representation change measures how the changes among the seven states persist across subsequent Transformer blocks. Third, temporal-state coordination and trajectory topology characterize when the commitment and verification occur relative to the support, and how the dominant state sequence evolves over the full inference process. Finally, we evaluate CauTrace on both clean reasoning failures and paired adversarial perturbations. Across Qwen and LLaMA-family models, the failed traces show weaker Attention-MLP agreement on support-state updates and less verification activity relative to commitment, while the exact representation-level signatures and timing shifts vary by architecture. Held-out repair and steering tests demonstrate consistent operational signals that were in line with our claims for certain models and specific settings, with aligned steering producing the predicted directional changes in process measures. Overall, CauTrace provides a unified diagnostic framework for analyzing failure dynamics through changes in support, commitment, and verification, which would shed light on the in-depth research on LLM security.

items.title: Understanding Everyday Communication Patterns, Stress, and Productivity in Hybrid Work through Egocentric Wearable Audio Sensing
items.abstract: The hybrid work trend in the post-COVID period has transformed how people communicate while at work. However, there is a lack of quantitative understanding of how home and office environments shape communicative behavior and affective well-being. To study this, as a part of a larger study of the role of work environment on stress, we designed an egocentric wearable audio sensing system that captured interpersonal communication across both working locations. The system extracts real-time acoustic features on a wearable audio sensor and performs offline foreground speaker diarization to derive speaking load and activeness features. To improve diarization performance under low-dimensional feature constraints, we apply a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework that transfers knowledge from large-scale speech foundation models into a compact ResNet-based model, achieving consistent improvements in diarization performance over the baseline across three public egocentric speech datasets. In a four-month longitudinal deployment with 16 participants, our system revealed location-dependent differences in work communication patterns. Moreover, the mixed linear model analyses showed that office-based speaking load was significantly associated with higher self-reported stress and lower self-reported productivity, while speaking activeness during home-based work amplified both productivity and affective load in this cohort.

items.title: Uneven Use, Similar Trust Generative AI in Denmark and Romania
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has spread unevenly across Europe, and it is unclear whether higher use brings higher trust. This paper compares Denmark and Romania, the EU's highest and lowest GenAI users, and asks whether the difference in public and institutional trust between them corresponds to the difference in trust in AI. Drawing on trust, technology-acceptance and digital-divide theory, it is a descriptive, contrasting-case analysis of harmonised data: GenAI usage comes from Eurostat, trust in AI more generally from the KPMG/Melbourne global study and public and institutional trust from the Standard Eurobarometer. In 2025, 48.4% of Danes aged 16-74 had used GenAI in the past three months, against 17.8% of Romanians. Use falls with age and rises with education in both countries, and the relative gaps are far larger in Romania; the patterns remain visible within the published age-by-education categories. Trust in AI does not follow usage: Romanians trust AI as much as Danes or slightly more, although Denmark leads by 28 to 45 percentage points on trust in government, parliament and the legal system. The Denmark-Romania comparison thus does not support a simple country-level correspondence between general institutional trust and trust in AI; in KPMG's pooled model, trust in AI is tied most closely to confidence in AI governance. The observed usage difference is more consistent with disparities in general digital skills and opportunities for work- and education-related use than with differences in trust. However, the available data cannot identify the independent effects of these factors. The results rest on two cases and non-identical constructs, and call for comparable microdata and disclosure experiments.

items.title: Urban housing and ageing in place: a preliminary study of spatial ergonomics in residential interiors for older adults in India
items.abstract: Purpose The population of older adults is growing rapidly and “ageing-in-place” has become the dominant living arrangement in India. Yet residential interiors in urban environments for older adults continue to be designed on Western anthropometric standards that overlook the physical and cultural needs of older Indians. This study aims to be a preliminary examination of the spatial ergonomics of the “Critical Triad” of kitchen, bedroom and toilet in urban homes in Tamil Nadu, India. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-method study was conducted with 30 participants (24 elderly and 6 middle-aged occupants) across Coimbatore, Salem and Vellore cities of Tamil Nadu, India. Data were collected through on-site spatial measurement, behavioural mapping, semi-structured interviews and expert photography and analysed using prevalence ranking and chi-square tests of association. Findings The study found extensive body-space mismatch rooted in Western-derived design dimensions. Ninety percent of elderly women reported physical strain while working in modular kitchens, 87% of participants lived with fear of falling in toilets and all participants reported discomfort from glossy bedroom flooring and inadequate circulation space. Chi-square analysis confirmed that several kitchen hazards (grinder use, prolonged standing, slippery flooring) are significantly gendered, while bedroom and toilet hazards affect both genders comparably. The erosion of traditional South Indian features such as verandas, detached toilets and semi-open kitchens was linked to heightened safety anxiety and physical dependency. Originality/value The study derives age-adjusted anthropometric benchmarks from National Institute of Design data and translates them into measurable architectural parameters and room layouts for the Critical Triad, offering designers an evidence-based, culturally grounded framework for age-responsive housing in South India.

items.title: VGIQA: Fine-Grained Image Quality Assessment with Visual Grounding Rewards
items.abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) aims to evaluate the perceptual visual quality of images. Recently, the rapid development of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has significantly advanced the IQA field. By integrating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and reinforcement learning (RL), these models can generate more accurate and interpretable results while relying on less training data. However, existing MLLM-based methods are predominantly constrained to holistic, image-level evaluations and lack the capability to produce fine-grained, localized assessments, which substantially limits their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose VGIQA, a novel IQA model endowed with both local and global quality assessment capabilities. VGIQA is trained via a two-stage paradigm comprising a cold-start phase followed by reinforcement learning. Driven by carefully designed local quality assessment reward functions, our model exhibits exceptional image quality understanding on VGSR-2K, a new dataset we propose specifically for local quality evaluation, significantly outperforming existing open-source MLLMs such as Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct. Furthermore, the local quality evaluation task can effectively enhance the model's performance on the degradation perception task.

items.title: vibe‐qc : An Open‐Source, General‐Purpose Electronic‐Structure Code for Molecules and Solids Developed With Generative AI
items.abstract: ABSTRACT We present vibe‐qc , a general‐purpose open‐source electronic‐structure code for molecules and solids, developed almost entirely with agentic AI under expert human direction. The code is released under the Mozilla Public License 2.0 (MPLv2). The implementation comprises a C++17 numerical core and Python calculation drivers. Molecular methods include Hartree–Fock, Kohn–Sham DFT, Møller–Plesset theory and double hybrids, coupled cluster, active‐space methods, and excited states. Dispersion corrections, continuum solvation, and effective core potentials are also available. Periodic calculations use Gaussian‐basis HF and DFT with Brillouin‐zone sampling. Molecular and periodic method coverage differs; the feature matrices specify analytic and numerical derivatives and distinguish validated and experimental implementations. The validation set is a key contribution of this work. It combines independent program comparisons, published benchmarks, and internal consistency tests. Molecular mean‐field energies agree at the nanohartree scale, and conventional CCSD(T) energies agree within for the tested systems. Local‐correlation and periodic limitations are reported with the comparisons. Numerical results, calculation metadata, and analysis scripts are supplied as machine‐readable . The independently maintained vibe‐view viewer, vibe‐queue scheduler, and qvf toolkit support visualization and job management; trexio provides wavefunction interchange.

items.title: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence
items.abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, language-based reasoning traces do not provide a reliable mechanism for models to revisit relevant visual evidence, leading to visual forgetting and impairing their ability to reason over video content. Existing approaches maintain visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways: they either refer to evidence using textual coordinates, which specify symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself, or reinsert cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, preserving visual details at the cost of substantial context expansion. To address these limitations, we introduce VideoLVR, which constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, thereby providing visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. To supervise latent visual evidence generation, we introduce a visual token prediction objective that formulates visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, thereby unifying visual evidence reconstruction and text generation within the same token prediction framework. This shared prediction framework enables MLLMs to reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. We further extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. By efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context. Experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, especially on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.

items.title: Virtual fencing and herding to manage grazing cattle
items.abstract: Virtual fencing (VF) and herding (VH) technologies are revolutionising the management of grazing cattle. These technologies use GPS-enabled collars to manage and contain cattle primarily with audio or vibration cues to guide behaviour, followed by electric shocks if the primary cues are ignored. This reduces the need for electric or physical fencing and decreases the labour required to move animals. This chapter reviews the development, application, and welfare implications of VF and VH technologies. Research and commercial experience demonstrate the effectiveness of the technology, with benefits including improved pasture utilisation, animal productivity, environmental stewardship, labour efficiency, and workforce satisfaction. New technologies must also demonstrate that they at least preserve, if not improve, animal welfare. VF technologies must include proper training regimes based on learning theory, safeguards to prevent the receipt of unpredictable or uncontrollable shocks, and be of an appropriate ergonomic design.

items.title: Virtual monitors and desktops: a pictorial essay on what radiodiagnosis could become
items.abstract: Radiology has evolved with technological innovation, and virtual reality (VR) is an emerging tool in diagnostic imaging workflows. This pictorial essay explores VR-based workstations and virtual monitors in radiology. It describes how immersive environments may complement conventional reading rooms. VR head-mounted displays (HMDs) enable customizable three-dimensional workspaces where radiologists can view multiple virtual monitors, modify spatial layouts, and collaborate remotely in real time. Current applications, including web-based picture archiving and communication system (PACS) platforms and integrated remote desktop functionality, demonstrate the utility of image visualization and interpretation in immersive environments.Potential advantages include workspace flexibility, portability, reduced physical space requirements, and remote collaboration.However, important limitations include display resolution, luminance performance, field of view, image legibility, visual fatigue, and limited validation for diagnostic interpretation.Although preliminary evidence suggests comparable diagnostic performance between VR and conventional monitors for selected imaging tasks, available studies are limited.As VR technology evolves, immersive workstations may become complementary tools within radiology workflows and teleradiology environments.Further research is needed to assess diagnostic accuracy, ergonomic effects, workflow efficiency, user comfort, and cost-effectiveness before broader clinical implementation, and to establish appropriate technical standards for safe, reliable use in routine clinical practice.

items.title: What Survives Distillation? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of GPT-2 and DistilGPT-2
items.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large language models into compact students that preserve aggregate metrics, yet the mechanistic consequences of depth-reduction distillation remain largely uncharacterized. This work applies linear CKA, logit lens analysis, attention pattern decomposition, sparse autoencoder feature statistics, and activation patching to compare GPT-2 and its six-layer student DistilGPT-2 across two canonical circuits: the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) circuit and the Greater-Than (GT) circuit. The results reveal a compression-collapse dichotomy: the IOI circuit suffers complete mechanistic collapse (DistilGPT-2: 35.2% accuracy vs. 94.8%, zero name-mover preservation), while the GT circuit survives with 87.7% task performance recovery through active remapping of the teacher's layer-9 comparison head into student layer~4 (mean Pearson r = 0.945). These findings demonstrate that circuit compressibility governs mechanistic survival under distillation, and that aggregate metrics are insufficient diagnostics for circuit integrity.

items.title: What Victims Take Away: Attack Reuse and Defense Revision after Prompt-Injection Attacks
items.abstract: Attack logs and red-team reports show targets the attacks used against them, to help them repair their defenses. Prompt injections against large language models (LLMs) are plain text, so such records also hand targets a working copy. Drawing on social learning theory and work on the victim-offender overlap, we study what targets do with that copy in Tensor Trust, an online game whose players defended LLM-guarded accounts, attacked one another's, and could read every attack they received. Using all 563,349 attack records, we compare each received attack with matched attacks that circulated among similar players at the same moment but never reached the target. Reuse mainly followed success: within a week, targets attacked other players with 10.0% of the attacks that had broken their defense, versus 0.03% of matched attacks (adjusted difference: 8.8-10.0 percentage points). Near-misses, whose replies began with "access granted" but that scored as failures, were reused about as rarely as failures: reuse tracked whether an attack paid off, not how its reply read, consistent with payoff-biased social learning. Breaches were also followed by defense changes, after which same-family attacks became 24.5 percentage points less successful against the target, relative to other defenders. Reuse came mainly from players already attacking, not newcomers. Previously received texts accounted for 23.2% of the successful hijacks we analyze. The attack history thus served both repair and reuse; we derive testable hypotheses for how AI security tools should disclose attacks, such as describing the technique without the full text.

items.title: When Algorithmic Management Works: The Role of Perceived Algorithmic Fairness
items.abstract: Digital transformation has accelerated the adoption of algorithm-driven work environments, creating significant challenges for workforce management. Therefore, this study examines how algorithmic management affects employees competitive productivity through the mediator of career resilience, while perceived algorithmic fairness acts as the moderator. Using survey data from 475 employees of Malaysian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), this study employs a mixed-method approach, incorporating partial least squares structural equation Modeling for hypothesis testing and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) for additional insights. Our findings confirm that algorithmic management enhances employees competitive productivity through career resilience, with perceived algorithmic fairness strengthening this effect, supported by fsQCA. Practically, SMEs should prioritize transparent algorithmic management and resilience-building initiatives to enhance employee competitive productivity. Theoretically, this study advances sociotechnical systems literature by integrating algorithmic management, resilience, and perceived algorithmic fairness, extending Information Systems research on digital workplaces.

items.title: When All Rollouts Fail: Policy-Compatible Joint Decoding for Hard-Problem Reasoning
items.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) derives its learning signal from binary rewards via on-policy exploration and becomes a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning of large language models. Yet it faces a learning cliff on problems beyond model's current ability: when every rollout fails, the samples reveal nothing about a correct solution, and group-relative estimators (e.g., GRPO, RLOO) collapse the update to zero advantage. Expert trajectories offer a remedy, but they are incompatible with the current policy and often lie in the student's low-probability regions, so the surviving updates demand large parameter shifts and decay into surface-level imitation rather than transferable reasoning. We argue that a useful learning signal on hard problems must be both verifiably correct and sufficiently compatible with the current policy. We propose Policy-Compatible Reinforcement Learning (PICO), which performs distribution-constrained joint decoding: expert data guides decoding at the token level while preserving the student's relative token probabilities, and a dynamic top-k mechanism confines the sampling distribution under a finite divergence budget, yielding trajectories that are verified and policy-compatible by construction. These trajectories are optimized jointly with on-policy rollouts under a mixed-behavior objective that mitigates their distribution mismatch via importance sampling. Experiments across reasoning diverse datasets and agentic benchmarks demonstrate that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and prior off-policy baselines.

items.title: When Generative AI Helps and Hurts: Augmentation-Substitution Taxonomy and Recovery Pattern in University Students’ Experiences
items.abstract: Generative AI is now widely used in higher education, yet the same tool can produce positive and negative outcomes for the same user, and the reasons for this remain underexplored. Using technology affordance theory, this study develops an empirically grounded taxonomy of interaction mechanisms based on students’ retrospective accounts. The 71 participants, who began university after the public release of generative AI, completed surveys and reported 254 experiences through interviews and written reflections. Three key findings emerged: first, most students reported both positive and negative experiences, with no measured person-level trait robustly associated with experiential valence; second, 17 interaction mechanisms were identified, organized by whether AI complemented or replaced cognitive tasks; third, some students shifted from negative to more positive trajectories. Experiential valence thus appears more closely associated with interaction context than with person-level traits, although the evidence is retrospective rather than causal.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: When Rules Meet Learning Algorithms: Price Caps, Random Audits and the Persistence of Algorithmic Collusion
items.abstract: Pricing algorithms that learn by trial and error can sustain supra-competitive prices without communicating. We ask which market rules weaken this behaviour. A bibliometric mapping of 828 Scopus records on AI agents in strategic settings (2020–2026) shows that the field studies coordination and cooperation far more than economic design: competition and collusion appear in 1.4% of documents and mechanism design in 1.3%. We address this gap with a computational experiment. Two Q-learning agents set prices in a repeated Bertrand duopoly with logit demand, following the baseline of Calvano et al. (2020). We compare a no-intervention baseline with price caps, random audits with fines, and asymmetries between agents, using 500 independent sessions per condition (5,000 in total). The baseline replicates the benchmark: the collusion index reaches 0.852 (95% CI 0.842–0.862). Every intervention lowers collusion (Welch tests, p < 0.001), but threshold-based rules mainly relocate it. Under a 20% audit probability, only 0.4% of sessions price above the audited threshold, yet the collusion index stays at 0.575. Removing one agent’s memory, which removes its capacity to punish deviations, cuts collusion to 0.712, while learning-speed asymmetries barely matter. Rules that target punishment capacity, not price levels, deserve more attention from competition authorities.

items.title: When to Intervene? An Empirical Study of Errors and Self-Recovery in LLM Agents
items.abstract: LLM agents interact with Web services to perform tasks on users' behalf. Errors during these interactions can disrupt execution and prevent task completion, motivating external intervention. However, agents may self-recover through continued execution, raising the question of when to intervene and when to wait for self-recovery. We present an empirical study of errors and self-recovery in LLM agents. We construct ReInBench, a dataset containing 1,259 agent traces and 1,403 error events across computer-use and Web tasks. Our study examines how often and how quickly agents self-recover, how self-recovery relates to subsequent execution and task completion, and whether self-recovery can be predicted when an error occurs. We find that 725 error events self-recover, often within a few steps, with self-recovery performance differing across Execution LLMs. Self-recovery can also help agents recover from subsequent errors of the same type and support overall task completion. Intervention should therefore prioritize errors unlikely to self-recover, while allowing agents to continue when self-recovery is likely. Building on these empirical findings, we propose ReCoF, a method that predicts whether an error will self-recover to inform whether additional intervention is needed. ReCoF achieves an average relative improvement of 9.02% in Macro-F1 over the strongest baseline on ReInBench. Our code and data can be found at https://method-notes.github.io/ReCoF/.

items.title: When uncertainty quantification fails: structural vulnerabilities and corrections for selective prediction under clinical class imbalance
items.abstract: Background. Selective prediction systems improve the safety of clinical artificial intelligence by deferring ambiguous cases to human experts while automating high-confidence decisions. However, this safety mechanism relies entirely on the premise that uncertainty scores accurately reflect clinical ambiguity. In prognostic tasks characterized by severe class imbalance, where the clinical outcome of interest is a minority, this assumption breaks down. Standard uncertainty measures cease to capture clinically aligned ambiguity; instead, they become a proxy for class membership, systematically penalizing minority patients regardless of their individual predictive clarity. Results. Across 56 synthetic conditions and three neurodegenerative cohorts spanning severe class imbalance to near-balanced conditions (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's Disease, Alzheimer's Disease), our framework consistently maintained bounded, balanced risk across trajectories. In contrast, global metrics either collapsed minority Sensitivity or protected the minority at the expense of majority patients. Applying CCR with standard entropy fails to protect the minority because it breaks within-class monotonicity when tau=0.5. Combining CCR with threshold-aware metrics restores strict monotonicity, correctly identifies ambiguous patients, and safely mitigates minority exclusion. Conclusions. Under clinical class imbalance, standard uncertainty quantification measures dataset sparsity rather than clinical ambiguity, creating a systemic illusion of safety. This bias is a correctable structural flaw. Clinical pipelines deploying selective prediction under imbalance should adopt threshold-aligned uncertainty measures and class-stratified evaluation. This reduces class-specific risk imbalance, supporting safer selective prediction under the evaluated conditions without silently excluding the most vulnerable patients.

items.title: When Visual Evidence Is Insufficient: How Instructions, Post-Training, and Internal Activations Shape Refusal in Multimodal Language Models
items.abstract: For reliable deployment, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) should recognize when an image provides insufficient evidence to answer a question and withhold unsupported answers. Yet refusal alone is not necessarily evidence of such recognition: models may refuse because of unrelated safety constraints or without identifying the missing evidence. We study how refusal on visually unanswerable questions is shaped by three sources of control: inference-time instructions, post-training, and internal activation interventions. Across three MLLMs on the MoHoBench benchmark, we systematically manipulate the meaning and placement of refusal instructions, compare supervised and preference-based post-training, and intervene on a refusal-related activation direction derived from naturally answered and refused examples. We find that refusal is highly sensitive to both the meaning and placement of instructions, with model-specific changes at the sample level that are obscured by aggregate refusal rates. Evidence-aware and general refusal instructions have stronger effects than an intentionally mismatched safety instruction. Post-training produces larger increases in refusal, but can also induce responses that combine refusal language with attempted answers. In contrast, activation intervention produces smaller yet transferable changes across prompt conditions, without evidence of indiscriminate refusal on tested visually answerable samples. These findings show that refusal is jointly shaped by external instructions, post-training, and internal representations, highlighting the need to disentangle evidence recognition from a model's learned propensity to refuse.

items.title: Whose Carbon Is It Anyway? Exploring Household Dynamics in Sustainable Mobility Tracking
items.abstract: Transport behaviors are a major contributor to carbon emissions, and decisions are often made at the household level around what form of transport to take and when. Technology, primarily eco-feedback interfaces (EFIs) have been suggested to support users in making environmentally friendly choices. However, there is a lack in understanding of how the underlying social dynamics of households influence decisions around sustainable practices, particularly through the lens of mobility. To understand how to design technology to better support households in negotiating around sustainable mobility choices, the research team interviewed 21 participants across nine households, probing them with four low-fidelity mockups representative of EFIs from prior work. We found that the varied mobility-related responsibilities among household members, as well as varying perspectives on the environment, can cause friction in the utility of EFIs in the home. We suggest that designs can account for these factors through acknowledging varied roles and perspectives.

items.title: Will AI Solve It All? A Transnational Qualitative Investigation of AI’s Role in Human Needs Fulfillment
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly promoted as a transformative solution for addressing fundamental human needs and improving quality of life. However, limited empirical research examines what people expect from AI in relation to their needs and how current AI technologies are perceived to meet them. This study presents a transnational qualitative investigation of AI’s role in human needs fulfillment across six countries. Guided by Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, findings show that recurring concerns about inaccuracy, hallucination, and trust point to informational integrity as an emerging need in AI-mediated contexts. Participants also viewed AI as a supportive tool rather than a replacement for human agency and creativity. Cross-national patterns showed a shared desire for personalized, adaptive AI, while the domains participants emphasized varied by country, reflecting local priorities. This work underscores the need to ground AI evaluation in lived experience and expand theoretical perspectives to account for evolving dimensions of human needs.

items.title: Working from home as we age: balancing health with personal choices - a qualitative interview study
items.abstract: Background: With the rise of ageing populations across the globe, many countries have reviewed retirement age and strongly supported active ageing. In the United Kingdom, a third of the workforce is aged over 50 with many extending their working lives and retiring at later life. In this context, it is pertinent to understand how 'working from home' (WFH) can impact our health and wellbeing especially as we age. Objective: In this paper, we focus on how the prevalence of health conditions in people over 65 years old might affect their work practices and preferences. Methods: Fourteen interviews were conducted, nine with older people WFH with long-term health condition(s) predominantly engaged in voluntary work, and five healthcare professionals who advise older adults regarding WFH. Results: We thematically analysed the findings and found that often personal preferences overtake health considerations when setting up the home environment to work, disregarding the impact wrong posture and long work patterns might have on their health. Also, older adults often consider the available resources and the frequency of their work while there is a lack of awareness of guidelines for setting up a workspace at home, this could be particularly influenced by the voluntary nature of the work that most of our participants engaged in. Conclusion: We outline recommendations on WFH based on the review of ergonomic guidelines, past studies considering older adult needs and our qualitative findings. The recommendations balance health with personal choices, acknowledging the nature of work, the resources available for individual adaptations, the social aspects that individuals want to maintain at home and the impact on health conditions, being more practical and applicable to WFH as we age.

items.title: Your Agent Acts Differently When You're Around: How User Presence Changes Agent Behavior in Negotiation
items.abstract: LLM agents increasingly interact with other agents on behalf of users, yet how users in the loop affect their agents' behavior--for better or worse--remains poorly understood. We study this question through the lens of negotiation, where agents must represent users while strategically bargaining with other agents. To isolate the effect of user presence, we develop PRESENT, a controlled evaluation framework that compares negotiation settings with and without an interactive user, while holding the game, objectives, and user preferences fixed across conditions. Across 11.2k runs spanning 7 games and 8 models, we find that user presence significantly changes both outcomes and behavior. Specifically, negotiation parties with a user obtain higher payouts (+13.7% on average) and their agents negotiate more aggressively. Surprisingly, user presence also induces misaligned behavior, both toward counterparties (where its rate roughly doubles) and toward users (where it emerges in 14.3% of games). These misaligned behaviors are uncorrelated with outcomes and persist even when the user sends only templated, neutral messages. These findings expose two blind spots in current evaluation practice: static instructions miss behaviors that emerge only when users are present, and outcome-level metrics cannot detect them.

items.title: “Completing” the State on the Eastern Frontier: Anthropology of Infrastructure and Grassroots Mobility Practices
items.abstract: The article explores the interaction between rotational (shift) workers and transport infrastructure in the remote regions of the Eastern Polygon and the Arctic, analyzing how grassroots practices “complete” state-led infrastructure projects. The study is based on 14 semi-structured interviews with residents of Buryatia engaged in long-term rotational work. Narrative analysis was employed within the theoretical frameworks of “sociotechnical assembly” and “materialized embodiment of relations”. The study identifies infrastructure as a dynamic environment that transforms citizens into “strategic assets” of the state. In extreme conditions, a physical symbiosis occurs between workers and machinery, resulting in a “human-robot” identity-a psychological adaptation to exhaustive 12-hour shifts. It is established that “infrastructural incompleteness” (e.g., lack of connectivity and domestic amenities) is compensated through “moral economy” practices, mutual aid, and autonomous household organization. The findings demonstrate that the rotational method (vakhta) fosters a specific mentality of “delayed life,” where social space is structured by the temporality of waiting and a habitual state of forced mobility. The study provides the first conceptualization of the “state completion” phenomenon by local actors on Russia’s eastern frontier, shifting the focus from the road as a technical object to a space that produces new forms of subjectivity. items.title: “I Am Surrounded!”: Decision-Making Processes Associated With Spatiotemporal Patterns and Teammates’ Communication in a National Esports Championship
items.abstract: This case study explored the influence of opponents’ spatial density and teammates’ communications on decision-making in a competitive gaming setting (i.e., League of Legends) using a mixed method. In-game behavior recordings complemented by verbal data from 15 post-game video-cued recall interviews were collected from five expert players during three French national Esport championship games. Using the Recognition-Primed Decision model, 243 decisions were classified into three types of recognition processes, and 70 decisions were observed to be influenced by teammate communication. Two distinct spatiotemporal game patterns emerged from data analysis. Decision processes seem to be affected by opponents’ spatial density and exhibit similarities to those observed in traditional team sports’ contexts, regardless of the level of time pressure involved. During higher spatial density phases, influenced decisions predominantly rely on sole reactions to explicit communication. Conversely, communications are mostly used as an auxiliary source of information in low spatial density phases. A quantitative increase in the cognitive package verbalization during confrontation phases introduces a potential paradox. Unlike traditional models suggesting a reduction in information quantity processed under pressure, high environmental monitoring and dense internal processing was observed, suggesting a complex micro-cognitive adaptation to manage increased proximal stimuli.

items.title: 5G-enabled Smart Hospitals
items.abstract: Smart hospitals are the pinnacle of healthcare innovation, transforming patient care and facility administration with cutting-edge technologies. This chapter addresses the pressing need for smart hospitals to successfully implement 5G technology in order to enhance patient outcomes, increase connectivity, and increase operational efficiency. A comprehensive review of the corpus of recent research, case studies, and professional comments are all part of the technique utilized to investigate how 5G will affect various aspects of smart hospital operations. The chapter highlights how 5G technology will enable telemedicine, remote monitoring, and real-time data analytics, thereby revolutionizing healthcare delivery. Medical professionals may work together and communicate more easily because of 5G’s features including high-speed, low-latency connectivity, which enhances patient care, diagnosis, and treatment. Smart hospitals can leverage AI-based technologies for predictive analytics, customized care, and enhanced patient involvement as a result of 5G adoption. The article also examines the potential benefits of 5G-enabled smart hospitals for disaster preparedness and emergency response. Case studies and examples demonstrate how 5G technology may improve situational awareness, coordinate resources, and deliver timely care during pandemics and natural disasters. Considering all of this, this chapter highlights how 5G technology will change smart hospitals and how crucial it is to welcome innovation in order to satisfy changing patient and community needs. A new era of healthcare delivery marked by improved connectivity, better patient outcomes, and unmatched efficiency may be ushered in by smart hospitals utilizing 5G technology.

items.title: 6G Technology Overview
items.abstract: The development of the sixth-generation (6G) wireless network is more groundbreaking than any other communication technology in history. It shows unmatched potential that will change the way healthcare is provided in Society 5.0. The author gives a thorough overview of the main features of 6G technology in this chapter, along with some examples of how it can be used in the health field. People think that 6G networks will have ultra-low latency communication with response times of less than a millisecond, huge connectivity with up to 10 million devices per square kilometer, and data rates higher than a terabyte. These features make it possible for very medical uses like real-time remote surgery, immersive extended reality medical training, smart Internet of Medical Things ecosystems, and AI-enabled healthcare predictive analytics. The combination of artificial intelligence at the network edge, holographic communications and the digital twin technology open opportunities to personalized and precision medicine approaches. This chapter talks about the technical side of 6G technology, how it could change healthcare systems, and the problems and chances that come with using 6G-enabled solutions in smart healthcare as part of the bigger picture of Society 5.0’s human-centered technological integration.

items.title: A Bibliometric and Network Analysis of Statistical Distributions in Machine Learning
items.abstract: Statistical distributions constitute a fundamental component of machine learning by providing the probabilistic framework required for modelling uncertainty, variability, and data-generating processes. They underpin a wide range of methodologies, including Bayesian inference, probabilistic graphical models, generative learning and uncertainty-aware artificial intelligence. Despite their widespread application, the evolution and intellectual structure of research on statistical distributions in machine learning have not been systematically examined. This study presents a bibliometric and network analysis of 840 Scopus-indexed publications published between 1997 and 2025. Bibliographic data were analysed using Biblioshiny and VOS viewer to evaluate publication trends, influential sources, author productivity, collaboration patterns and thematic developments. Descriptive indicators were complemented by co-authorship, co-citation, keyword co-occurrence and thematic analyses to explore the social and intellectual structure of the field. The findings reveal sustained growth in research output, increasing international collaboration and the dominance of a core set of journals and authors. Network analyses identify probabilistic modelling, Bayesian learning, uncertainty quantification and generative approaches as the principal intellectual foundations of the field. The results further indicate a gradual shift from classical statistical learning frameworks toward uncertainty-aware and explainable machine learning paradigms. By mapping the evolution, knowledge structure and emerging directions of this research domain, the study provides a comprehensive reference for future investigations at the intersection of statistical distribution theory and machine learning.

items.title: A Certified Robustness Framework for Backdoor Poisoning Attacks using $f$-Divergences
items.abstract: Machine learning systems trained on untrusted data are vulnerable to data and backdoor poisoning attacks, in which an adversary corrupts training and test samples to manipulate predictions at inference time. Randomized smoothing yields provable defenses against such attacks, but existing applications to train-time robustness are limited to specific threat models and smoothing mechanisms. We propose a general framework that allows expressing complex adversary constraints on the number of corrupted training examples, feature and label perturbation magnitudes, and test-time corruptions. Our framework randomizes inputs by combining data subsampling with feature, label and test-sample noising. We develop a composable certification procedure based on $f$-divergences that handles arbitrary combinations of threat models and noising strategies, and recovers several prior certification regimes exactly as special cases. We demonstrate our framework experimentally by certifying, for the first time, robustness under general $\ell_p$-constrained poisoning adversaries under bagging with additive Laplace, Gaussian, and Uniform noises.

items.title: A decision-function framework for auditing artificial decision-makers: Evidence from an immigration conjoint benchmark
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to stand in for survey respondents and other human decision-makers, but agreement in average responses can mask different ways of weighting case attributes. We propose a decision-function framework that compares human and model outputs at the level of conditional response patterns and calibrates subgroup comparisons against the recoverability of the human target. Using a U.S. immigration conjoint benchmark and matched GPT, Qwen, and Llama evaluations, we find that no-persona LLMs reproduce much of the overall human applicant-weighting pattern while placing greater weight on several features that map readily onto administrative categories. GPT persona prompts show less consistent subgroup correspondence: education, in-group preference, and party depart most consistently from recoverable human subgroup patterns, whereas ideology and income vary across roles and outcomes. Within GPT, prompt-defined role frames also shift persona-conditioned weights. Together, these results show that human–LLM correspondence depends on the comparison being made and, for subgroup claims, on how reliably the human target itself can be recovered.

items.title: A double-edged sword of AI in agri-food production: how production methods shape consumers' purchase intention
items.abstract: Purpose Drawing on technology acceptance theory and innovation resistance theory, this study systematically investigates how production methods (artificial intelligence (AI) vs traditional) in agri-food production influence consumers' purchase intention. Design/methodology/approach Three experimental studies were conducted. Study 1 validated the main effect of production methods on purchase intention. Study 2 revealed the dual mediating roles of perceived novelty and perceived naturalness in this relationship. Study 3 examined the moderating role of food atypicality. Findings AI (vs traditional) production methods increase perceived novelty but undermine perceived naturalness of agri-food. Due to negativity bias, the negative path dominates the positive path, leading to an overall negative main effect on purchase intention. Moreover, these effects are moderated by food atypicality: for atypical food, purchase intention for AI-produced agri-food is enhanced via perceived novelty; while for typical food, purchase intention for traditionally produced options is enhanced via perceived naturalness. Originality/value First, this research expands the AI marketing literature by shifting the predominant research perspective from human–AI social interactions to customers' inferences about food's natural attributes. Second, it integrates technology acceptance theories to identify the dual roles of perceived naturalness and perceived novelty in the evaluation of AI-produced agri-food, as well as the dominance of negative perceptions in this evaluation process. Third, this study introduces food atypicality as a boundary condition to reveal differing consumer response patterns.

items.title: A Dual-Loop Decision Support System for AIGC-Driven FMCG Print Advertisement Creative Generation
items.abstract: Creative decision-making under time pressure suffers from inefficient human–artificial intelligence (AI) collaboration and weak evaluation feedback. This paper proposes a dual-loop decision support system that integrates prompt diffusion, human-in-the-loop fine-tuning, and real-time multi-criteria scoring. Validated on print advertisement creatives from three fast-moving consumer goods brands using campaign logs, graphics processing unit records, and crowd ratings, the system achieves improved performance against end-to-end AI-generated content while maintaining creative diversity and brand alignment. Built-in feedback controls including anomaly rollback and version archiving optimize convergence processes and reduce computing resource consumption per project. The results confirm that structured human–AI iteration enhances both the speed and the quality of creative decisions, offering a robust, replicable decision support system architecture for intelligent content generation.

items.title: A Good-Practice Example for Teaching Generative Artificial Intelligence Competencies to (Future) Adult Educators
items.abstract: This article outlines the development and revision process of a good-practice example for a university seminar for adult education master’s students in Germany to teach Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) competencies. Through an examination of the discourse on the digital and GenAI divide, the necessary prerequisites for ac­quiring GenAI competencies are drawn upon and integrated into the seminar design. The article also traces how the module plan has evolved over the years based on evaluations and technological developments. Drawing on GenAI competency models and Freire’s pedagogy, the seminar’s primary aim is to provide students with a critical understanding of GenAI. Drawing on anonymous and personal feedback from students, the seminar has been refined continuously between 2023 and 2026, and is currently in its fifth iteration. Experience has shown that teaching a critical approach to GenAI is most effective through an examination format in which students create a future professional activity exclusively using GenAI.

items.title: A Humanistic Approach to Classroom Management to Enhance Student Discipline at SMPIT Insan Mandiri Grenville, Bekasi Regency
items.abstract: This study aims to describe strategies for improving student discipline, identify the steps involved in implementing a humanistic approach to classroom management, and analyze the contribution of the humanistic approach to enhancing student discipline at SMPIT Insan Mandiri Greenville, Bekasi Regency. This study employed a qualitative approach using a case study method. The participants consisted of five teachers, five students, the school's Director of Education, and students’ parents. Data were collected through interviews, observations, and document analysis. The data were analyzed using the Miles and Huberman model, which includes data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings of this study reveal several important points. First, strategies for improving student discipline were implemented through establishing clear goals and fostering an understanding of the meaning of discipline, developing positive habits, providing teacher role models, applying educational rules and consequences, and strengthening intrinsic motivation through a personal approach. Second, the implementation of the humanistic approach to classroom management was carried out by providing students with autonomy and opportunities for participation, promoting empathetic and open communication, encouraging collaborative learning, respecting individual differences, integrating emotional and cognitive aspects into the learning process, and conducting reflective and constructive evaluations. Third, the humanistic approach contributed positively to the improvement of student discipline, as reflected in the development of intrinsic discipline, increased self-control, responsibility, learning motivation, and more positive relationships between teachers and students. The findings also indicate that discipline developed through a humanistic approach tends to be more sustainable because it is rooted in self-awareness rather than merely in supervision or punishment. In conclusion, the humanistic approach to classroom management at SMPIT Insan Mandiri Greenville contributes positively to improving student discipline. The implementation of this approach not only helps create a conducive and humane classroom environment but also promotes the development of discipline based on students’ self-awareness, making it more sustainable in their daily lives.

items.title: A hybrid approach to evaluating mental health indicators and predicting student mental health risk
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines relational closeness between university students' academic achievement, represented by cumulative grade point average (CGPA) and mental health, well-being, sociodemographic variables using a self-reported student survey. Anxiety, depression, stress, sleep quality, diet quality, physical energy level, age, gender, department and scholarship status were analyzed. Relational and predictive relevance was evaluated without assuming causality, with an ergonomic interpretation of well-being indicators. Design/methodology/approach Grey relational analysis (GRA) estimated relational degrees between CGPA and selected variables. Deng's, absolute, relative, comprehensive and negative GRA models were applied, with sensitivity analyses across distinguishing coefficient values. Cronbach's alpha and exploratory factor analysis (EFA) examined whether anxiety, depression and stress represented a common structure. They were combined into a risk construct defined as “mental health risk.” Seven machine learning algorithms classified this construct. Repeated randomized train-test experiments assessed accuracy, precision, F1-score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) area under the curve (AUC). Findings Anxiety, depression and stress showed relatively high relational degrees with CGPA compared with the other variables. These findings suggest that academic achievement is related not only to demographic characteristics but also to psychological well-being and ergonomics-related conditions of students. According to the machine learning results, AdaBoost achieved the highest mental health risk classification performance, with an accuracy of 82.98%. Originality/value This study integrates comparative GRA modeling, statistical construction of a mental health risk indicator, repeated machine learning evaluation and ergonomic interpretation. The framework links relational analysis with predictive classification while distinguishing analytical risk from clinical diagnosis.

items.title: A Hybrid Framework for Explainable Aviation Risk: Causal Chain Extraction from Safety Reports with Physics-Based Failure Quantification and Interventional Analysis
items.abstract: Aviation authorities hold decades of accident reports whose narratives record how investigators reconstructed each accident. Computational work on these archives has mostly sorted reports into fixed taxonomies. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework in which a text-based corpus identifies the leading factors of a failure mode. Physics-based models then quantify how likely that failure is at a stated operating point. Ordered causal chains extracted from 56,202 American accident reports with a local large language model aggregate into a causation knowledge graph. On an evaluation sample of 2,000 reports, the chains recover 90.8% of investigator-flagged causes. Each physical factor whose drivers the record carries receives an occurrence model calibrated to the accident population. A leaky noisy-OR fitted to the corpus combines the factors into a failure mode probability that supports intervention. For engine power loss, the carburetor icing model separates 1,205 icing accidents from other accidents using temperature and dewpoint alone, reaching 0.61 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve against a density ratio ceiling of 0.64. Routine weather hours give no valid control, because flying concentrates in fair weather. On later years the physics adds 0.03 to that area for occurrence and nothing for severity, so its value lies in interpretability. On four named accidents, abduction gives a probability of necessity of 0.29 to 0.50 for the heat omission, under monotonicity. The Fast Causal Inference algorithm does not license the largest backdoor adjustment on the learned networks.

items.title: A JiT-Based Denoising Defense Method Against Adversarial Examples for Radio Signal Automatic Modulation Classification
items.abstract: Automatic modulation classification (AMC) of radio signals is a core technology for spectrum monitoring and electromagnetic situational awareness. Deep neural networks (DNNs) play an important role in this field owing to their powerful feature extraction capabilities and end-to-end learning paradigm. However, their vulnerability to adversarial attacks poses serious security challenges to practical deployment. Adversarial training, a common defense, has limitations including poor generalization across attack types and high training costs. Inspired by Just image Transformers (JiT), a diffusion generative model that directly predicts clean images, this paper proposes a JiT-based denoising defense against adversarial examples for radio signal modulation classification. During training, a signal-specific 1D Transformer denoising network is optimized via flow matching to directly predict clean signal samples. It thereby learns a mapping that projects arbitrary examples back onto the low-dimensional manifold of clean signal examples. During inference, arbitrary examples are fed into the trained network and directly projected onto this manifold. This enables denoising defense without prior knowledge of attacks. Experiments on the RML2018.01A dataset were conducted without attack information, using a single empirically selected, fixed denoising start time. Compared with PGD-based adversarial training, the proposed method achieves a relative improvement of at least 20.58% in robust accuracy under PGD attacks. It also achieves a relative improvement of 10.20% in classification accuracy on clean examples. When evaluated against attack types unseen during adversarial training, the proposed method provides stronger defense than adversarial training. In particular, at higher attack strengths, it achieves a relative improvement of at least 39.72% in robust accuracy.

items.title: A macro-model for smart city development using citizens’ perspective: evidence from Indian smart cities
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop and empirically validate a citizen-centric macro-model for smart city development (SCD) in the Indian context. A climate-responsive conceptual overlay, derived from literature synthesis, is presented alongside the tested model but is not itself empirically tested. The study addresses the technology-centric construction of existing smart city frameworks and the limited integration of citizen-defined, cross-cutting property of urban systems, asking citizens how smart city dimensions relate to SCD and quality of life (QOL), and how citizen participation (CP) and support orientation (SO) moderate these relationships. Design/methodology/approach A sequential mixed-methods design is used. Phase 1 applies thematic analysis to 41 citizen interviews across 22 Indian smart cities, yielding 19 factors organised into eight aggregate dimensions; a ninth dimension (smart living) is added from the literature, and climate-responsive factors are integrated through literature synthesis. Phase 2 tests the macro-model through PLS-SEM on primary survey data from 491 respondents, with CP and SO as moderators. Findings The structural model establishes a strong pathway from SCD to QOL, with smart people as the strongest direct predictor of SCD. Smart environment and smart sustainable design, the two dimensions most closely linked to climate responsiveness in the conceptual integration, are non-significant as direct predictors. Smart environment is significant only at high levels of both CP and SO, while smart sustainable design is significant only at high levels of SO. CP moderates the majority of dimensional effects, and combined CP + SO moderation produces the largest explanatory gain, repositioning smart city dimensional effects as conditional rather than linear-additive. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional Indian design limits causal inference and cross-national generalisability. The findings reposition smart cities as citizen-conditioned sociotechnical systems and establish moderation analysis as a substantive theoretical commitment. Practical implications Technical smart city investments must be coupled with CP mechanisms. The dimensions most closely associated with climate responsiveness require both participatory engagement and institutional support to deliver citizen-perceived value. The evaluation frameworks should shift from aggregate output metrics to citizen-reported outcomes. Originality/value This study offers the first citizen-derived smart city macro-model for the Indian context, validated through PLS-SEM with participation and institution-based moderators; this tested model constitutes the study’s empirical contribution. The accompanying climate-responsive integration is a conceptual overlay derived from literature synthesis, offered as a framework for future testing rather than as a validated result.
