items.title: A phenomenological inquiry into supporting and hindering factors of Palestinian teacher wellbeing under military occupation in the West Bank and East Jerusalem
items.abstract: Teacher wellbeing under military occupation represents a fundamentally understudied dimension of occupational health in conflict-affected settings. While existing research predominantly emerges from contexts of relative stability, Palestinian educators in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem navigate a fragmented reality shaped by prolonged military occupation, territorial fragmentation, movement restrictions, and differential legal systems. Guided by positive psychology and structural violence theory, this phenomenological study explored both supporting and hindering factors influencing teacher wellbeing in the occupied Palestinian territory. Data were collected using a phenomenological design with purposive and snowball sampling to recruit 23 Palestinian teachers across four geographic zones: Urban West Bank (Area A), Rural West Bank/Area C, East Jerusalem, and UNRWA refugee camps. Data collection incorporated methodological triangulation via semi-structured interviews, focus groups, and narrative frames. Participants described key supporting factors as collective resilience and peer solidarity (pedagogical sumud), professional identity and moral purpose, community recognition and cultural value of education, and adaptive coping strategies. Conversely, participants identified significant hindering factors as geographically differentiated trauma exposure, institutional fragmentation and inconsistent support systems, checkpoint-related stress and mobility restrictions, curriculum constraints and professional ethical distress, and material insecurity. Teachers articulated that their wellbeing was significantly enhanced by strong collegial bonds, community appreciation, and sense of professional mission. However, participants perceived that daily exposure to checkpoints, administrative fragmentation, forced displacement threats, economic precarity, and systemic constraints on professional autonomy severely diminished their wellbeing and capacity to teach effectively. The findings contribute to understanding teacher wellbeing within frameworks of positive psychology and structural violence, indicating that promoting support-related factors while addressing occupation-induced hindering factors can ultimately enhance both teacher experiences and educational outcomes in protracted conflict contexts.

items.title: A Qualitative Study to Explore Delirium Management and Capability Building in Nurses Caring for Older Patients With Complex Care Needs in the Acute Hospital Setting
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Nurse-led strategies are important for preventing delirium and minimising its consequences when it occurs. Expertise in managing behavioural disturbances not only ensures safe care but also provides opportunities to mentor novice nurses. It is, however, important to know more about nurses' experiences caring for people with delirium to improve support for nurses caring for patients with complex care needs. AIMS: To explore the experience of nursing patients with delirium in the acute hospital setting. DESIGN: Descriptive qualitative study. METHODS: Nurses from two acute aged health wards in a Sydney metropolitan tertiary hospital participated in a semi-structured interview. Eleven interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were qualitatively analysed by directed content analytical method using human factors principles as an interpretative lens. FINDINGS: The interaction of multiple human factors was identified under the 'people', 'management' and 'workplace' framework. Participants identified barriers to delirium management, such as inadequate workforce capability and limited opportunities for novice nurses to develop expertise in delirium management, deficiencies in the environment and information technology and inflexible roles within the multidisciplinary team, leading to a high burden of care for nurses. Most had experienced difficulties delivering patient and family-centred care stemming from excessive workloads and a lack of structured mentorship. CONCLUSION: Our study identified substantial challenges faced by nurses caring for patients with delirium in the acute care setting. It also highlighted the complexity of delirium care and the importance of clinical expertise, skills development and the capacity for nurses to mentor other nurses. IMPLICATIONS: Healthcare organizations need to ensure that nurses with expertise in the care of older patients with complex care needs are available to provide comprehensive, patient- and family-centred care and provide mentorship and support to less experienced nurses. Interdisciplinary workforce capability building should be a priority. IMPACT: This study contributes to addressing the multidisciplinary management of patients with delirium in acute settings. The study found that delirium management is complex and requires a multidisciplinary workforce with knowledge, skills and adequate numbers. This research will have an impact on clinicians and health services managers in tailoring the care of patients and supporting the workforce. REPORTING METHOD: Adherence to the COREQ Checklist. items.title: A retrieval-augmented LoRA-Tuned LLM framework for structured software test case generation
items.abstract: Abstract Modern software systems are becoming increasingly complex that require scalable and reliable testing mechanisms for quality and robustness. The manual test case design remains a significant limitation as it is time-consuming, inconsistent, and prone to human error when dealing with large-scale and evolving requirements. The existing automated models struggle to generate structured, semantically coherent, and contextually relevant test cases which indicates the need for more intelligent and efficient solutions. This study proposes a novel Retrieval-Augmented and LoRA-tuned Large Language Model for automated generation of structured software test cases from textual requirements. The proposed model combines the FLAN-T5 with Retrieval-Augmented Generation to integrate the contextual grounding and Low-Rank Adaptation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning that allows the high-quality generation to maintain the computational efficiency. The proposed model is trained on a large-scale custom dataset that contain real-world test case records collected from enterprise tools such as Jira and Zephyr, and generates structured JSON-based test cases aligned with industrial standards. The enterprise-style structured test-case dataset and controlled experimental protocol used in this study. The proposed configuration achieved a BLEU score of 0.5897, ROUGE-L of 0.8095, BERTScore F1 of 0.9679, and semantic cosine similarity of 0.9816. A duplicate rate of 0.000 and a hallucination rate of 0.017 were also observed under the defined evaluation criteria. The results indicate the potential of retrieval augmentation and parameter-efficient fine-tuning for structured test-case generation within the investigated setting. The enterprise dataset and trained artifacts are restricted and findings interpreted within the scope of the evaluated task rather than as evidence of universal performance superiority. The integration of retrieval augmentation results in a mean inference latency of approximately 6·27s per test case indicates a measurable computational overhead with the improved contextual grounding. The findings show a practical performance between generation quality and inference efficiency within the evaluated enterprise-style test-case generation setting.

items.title: A Review of Outage Recovery Approaches for Enhancing Resilience in Electrical Distribution Systems
items.abstract: The increasing frequency and intensity of electrical outages in modern power distribution systems highlight the urgent need for resilient recovery mechanisms. In developing nations such as Nigeria, frequent system disturbances caused by extreme weather events, equipment failures, and inadequate grid automation have exposed the limitations of conventional restoration strategies. Resilient outage recovery models aim to restore power quickly, minimize service interruption, and maintain operational continuity under uncertain conditions. This review synthesizes recent advances in outage recovery frameworks, emphasizing resilience-based optimization, distributed intelligence, and network reconfiguration strategies. The paper also discusses enabling technologies such as artificial intelligence, Internet of Things (IoT) sensing, and microgrid integration, which collectively enhance situational awareness and adaptive control. Finally, the review highlights key research challenges and proposes directions for the next generation of resilient, data-driven recovery systems suitable for emerging distribution networks.

items.title: A Socratically Scaffolded Personal AI Mentor for Postdigital Lifelong Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are entering adult education without adequate andragogical grounding. This paper addresses that gap by developing an evidence-informed conceptual architecture for a Socratically scaffolded Personal AI Mentor in postdigital lifelong learning. The approach is conceptual framework development through theory-to-application translation, drawing on the author’s qualitative evidence synthesis (QES) of seven stud­ies of digital and e-mentoring in adult and professional learning. The theoretical base, grounded in Dewey’s pragmatism and transactional realism, integrates andragogy, transformative learning, critical inquiry, Socratic questioning, experiential learning, and social sustainability. The resulting architecture specifies six design compo­nents: goal-oriented engagement, a Socratic-Kolb inquiry process, a dialectic trace, resilient continuity, a human bridge, and agentic constraints. The paper concludes that AI mentoring should preserve learner agency, support reflective inquiry, sustain continuity, and connect learners to human communities.

items.title: A Survey of Knowledge Extraction Attacks and Defenses in LLM Agent Ecosystems
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in handling complex tasks. However, their development and deployment require substantial human and financial resources, making commercial LLM agents valuable intellectual property (IP) assets and raising concerns about their protection. In particular, knowledge extraction (KE) attacks aim to recover protected knowledge or replicate agent components and functionalities without authorization, posing threats to intellectual property and user privacy. Existing surveys primarily focus on model extraction or address information leakage as part of broader security discussions, leaving knowledge extraction across the LLM-based agent ecosystem insufficiently explored. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic survey of knowledge extraction attacks and defenses in LLM-based agents. We propose an asset-oriented taxonomy that categorizes protected knowledge into three groups: agent training assets, deployment-integrated assets, and runtime reusable assets, encompassing training data, LLMs, prompts, RAG systems, agent memory, and skills. For each category, we systematically examine representative attack mechanisms and corresponding defenses, identifying recent advances and outstanding challenges. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of knowledge extraction threats and inspire future research toward more secure and trustworthy LLM-based agents.

items.title: A Systematic Review of Health Information Systems Evaluation Frameworks: Evolution, Dimensions and a Value-Based Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: This is a retrospective registration of a systematic literature review on health information system (HIS) evaluation frameworks. The review was conducted following the Kitchenham and Charters guidelines for systematic literature reviews and is reported according to PRISMA 2020. The protocol (research questions, PICOC, search strings, eligibility criteria, quality assessment criteria and data extraction form) was defined before screening; this registration was created after screening, quality assessment and data extraction had been completed. Objectives: (1) to analyse the evolution of HIS evaluation approaches; (2) to develop a typology of existing frameworks; (3) to identify core evaluation dimensions and criteria; and (4) to propose a value-based conceptual framework for HIS evaluation. Research questions: RQ1 – What evaluation frameworks have been proposed for HIS? RQ2 – How have they evolved over time in concepts, methodologies and application contexts? RQ3 – What evaluation dimensions, criteria and indicators are commonly used? RQ4 – How do frameworks differ in strengths, limitations and applicability across healthcare contexts? RQ5 – What research gaps and methodological limitations remain? RQ6 – What value-based elements and emerging trends are present in the HIS evaluation literature? Methods: Nine databases (Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, Emerald, Taylor & Francis) were searched on 17–27 April 2026. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed English-language journal articles (2010 onwards) that proposed, adapted, applied or validated an HIS evaluation framework with explicit dimensions or criteria; reviews and conference papers were excluded. Title/abstract screening, full-text eligibility, quality assessment (six criteria, QA1–QA6) and data extraction (28 fields) were performed by a single human reviewer assisted by a large language model, with verification of all inclusions and a random sample of exclusions and calculation of Cohen's kappa. Data were synthesised narratively, with framework typology, harmonised evaluation dimensions, three-level value-based coverage rating and analysis by period (2010–2015, 2016–2020, 2021–2026). Expected outcomes: a typology and evolutionary analysis of HIS evaluation frameworks, a synthesis of evaluation dimensions, an appraisal of value-based coverage, and a proposed value-based HIS evaluation framework (VB-HISEF). Supporting materials (search strings, screening decisions, quality assessment and extraction dataset) will be shared as part of this registration.

items.title: A systematic review of human- and emerging AI-generated reformulation in L2 writing
items.abstract: Reformulation has long served as a feedback approach in second language (L2) writing. With the emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI), particularly ChatGPT, AI-generated reformulation has recently begun to appear in L2 writing research, although this area remains nascent. Guided by the PRISMA framework, this study reviews 26 empirical studies on reformulation in L2 writing published up to January 13, 2026. Unlike previous reviews of positive evidence feedback or model texts more broadly, this review provides a reformulation-focused synthesis and maps both human-generated and emerging AI-generated practices. The review focuses on three key dimensions: (1) research contexts and trends, (2) methodological characteristics, and (3) primary focus areas and key findings. Results indicate that: (1) research has predominantly targeted university-level English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners, with emerging interest in AI-generated feedback; (2) methodologies have mainly employed quasi-experimental designs situated in classroom-based, three-stage narrative tasks; and (3) while reformulation-only studies have tended to conceptualize writing as a process and emphasize learners’ attention to lexical and grammatical features, reformulation-integrated studies have produced mixed findings regarding the transition from cognitive processing to written products. These findings underscore the multifaceted role of reformulation in L2 writing development and identify critical directions for future research, particularly concerning the integration of emerging AI-assisted pedagogical practices.

items.title: A workflow-aligned framework for AI literacy in materials-informatics education: scientific judgment, equity, and curriculum design
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to predict materials properties, prioritize experiments, and generate hypotheses in materials science. The limiting challenge is no longer only algorithmic capability, but also whether students and educators can use AI with domain-specific scientific judgment. This conceptual analysis argues that AI education for AI-powered materials discovery should move beyond tool access and surface-level interaction with generative systems toward a workflow-aligned model of AI literacy. The analysis links AI literacy to core materials-informatics competencies: data provenance, domain-specific featurization, model validation, uncertainty quantification, physics-informed reasoning, reproducibility, and experimental feedback. It also advances an outcome-oriented equity perspective in which institutions evaluate not only access and participation, but also comparable learning gains, transfer of learning, learner confidence calibration, persistence, and research readiness across student subgroups. The article synthesizes relevant evidence, identifies cognitive and ethical risks such as off-loading and cognitive surrender, and proposes a dual-track curriculum model, implementation recommendations, reusable curriculum artifacts, and a set of testable propositions for future study. The central goal is to prepare students to become better scientists—not merely more efficient users of AI tools.

items.title: A1-Enabled Drug Discovery with Tulsi
items.abstract: Background: Ocimum tenuiflorum L. (syn. O. sanctum; Tulsi, holy basil) is a Lamiaceae herb central to Ayurveda and now a frequent subject of computational drug discovery. Objective: To review how artificial intelligence (AI) and related in silico methods have been applied to O. tenuiflorum over roughly the last five years, to separate what these studies show from what they do not, and to outline implications for society. Methods: A structured narrative review of recent literature (2021 to October 2026) was conducted using web-based searches, with older sources used only for background. Thirteen primary Tulsi-focused studies were charted by approach, target, disease area, and main finding. Findings: Most studies combine database mining (notably IMPPAT), ADMET filtering, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics with targets spanning diabetes (DPP4, GAPDH, PPARδ), cancer (EGFR), inflammatory disease (AKT1, STAT3), and SARS-CoV-2 main protease. A smaller, emerging group applies machine learning or deep learning to metabolomics, hyperspectral imaging, and multi-omics. Experimental or clinical validation is sparse. Human trial evidence is limited in scale, and a 2023 regulatory-style risk assessment raised reproductive-safety precautions. Conclusion: Tulsi is a credible source of hypotheses, not yet of validated drug leads. The field's priority is closing the loop between prediction, standardized extracts, wet-lab assays, and well-designed trials, while protecting traditional knowledge and consumers.

items.title: Academic Assessment and Integrity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This chapter examines the enduring challenge of academic integrity within the rapidly evolving landscape of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). While academic misconduct has long been described as “epidemic,” the COVID-19 pandemic and the advent of GenAI have profoundly amplified its scope and complexity. The pandemic's widespread adoption of summative online unsupervised remote (SOUR) assessments created fertile ground for cheating, while GenAI tools such as ChatGPT introduced unprecedented opportunities for students to outsource cognitive effort with ease, speed, and minimal risk of detection. Empirical evidence confirms that AI-assisted misconduct is now pervasive, raising urgent concerns about assessment validity and the erosion of core academic values. The chapter situates these developments within a historical and theoretical context, tracing shifts from traditional cheating to contract-based services and, ultimately, to AI-driven practices. It explores three levels of concern—individual, interpersonal, and institutional—highlighting cognitive offloading, character compromise, inequity, contagion effects, and reputational harm. These issues underscore that cheating is not merely a technical problem of validity but a moral and cultural challenge with far-reaching implications for education and society. Recognizing the limitations of detection-based approaches, the chapter advocates for systemic, proactive strategies. It introduces three complementary frameworks: the Swiss Cheese Model (layers of Environment, Engineering, Education, and Enforcement), the Educational Integrity Enforcement Pyramid (graduated interventions from self-regulation to command regulation), and the Two-Lane Assessment Approach (secured summative assessments prohibiting AI use alongside open formative tasks encouraging ethical AI integration). Together, these models offer a holistic response to the “wicked problem” of safeguarding integrity in an era where AI is ubiquitous and increasingly capable. The chapter concludes with a call to action for educators, institutions, and policymakers to reimagine assessment design, foster AI literacy, and cultivate cultures of trust and responsibility. Rather than attempting to eliminate AI from learning, the challenge lies in creating environments where integrity remains the most meaningful and rewarding path forward.

items.title: Acceso a la formación agraria virtual en comunidades rurales nicaragüenses
items.abstract: Digitalization in rural areas presents the challenge of moving beyond mere access to mobile devices to achieve meaningful educational appropriation. In Nicaragua, although there are valuable and successful institutional efforts in higher and technical education through national platforms, it is strategically important to complement these initiatives by adapting virtual learning environments to the sociotechnical dynamics of the agricultural sector. The objective of this study was to analyze the conditions of access to online learning to propose a context-based pedagogical model under the Education 3.0 paradigm. A mixed-methods approach was employed using a concurrent triangulation design, whose descriptive and cross-sectional purpose made it possible to establish a situational diagnosis by combining structured surveys administered to 123 students and agricultural producers affiliated with the Universidad Nacional Agraria. The results showed that 74.8% of users own smartphones and demonstrate high levels of motivation; however, 36.6% identified time constraints as their main challenge, and only 32.5% experience “nomadic connectivity.” The findings confirmed that academic equity requires moving beyond the uncritical transfer of urban instructional models. Therefore, to transform these barriers into opportunities for self-directed learning, it is imperative to transition toward a mobile learning ecosystem structured around low-data-consumption asynchronous microlearning units. The implementation of Learning Management Systems configured for offline study ensures equitable access to knowledge and strengthens technological autonomy without disrupting the productive cycles of rural communities.

items.title: ADACT: PDE-Constrained Thermal Hardware/Software Co-Design Adjoint-Driven Optimal Control via Finite Difference Discretization
items.abstract: By virtue of the sheer compute demands of large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC), modern multi-core microprocessors suffer from severe power density limits and thermal throttling, entailing an urgent need for principled methods for predictive, physics-informed dynamical thermal management (DTM). Here, we introduce a hardware/software co-design physics-informed PDE-constrained DTM throttling optimal control algorithm, ADACT (Adjoint-Driven Adaptive Co-Design Thermal Control), that minimizes thermal risk and cooling energy overhead while maximizing core execution throughput. The underlying physical temperature field is governed by a two-dimensional nonhomogeneous parabolic reaction-diffusion equation with spatially localized, time-varying power source terms and variable convective cooling subject to nonhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. We employ a discretization of the continuous state PDE via a Crank-Nicolson finite difference scheme with a 5-point discrete Laplacian operator on a uniform spatial mesh, which preserves unconditional numerical stability and $O(Δx^2 + Δy^2 + Δt^2)$ second-order temporal and spatial accuracy. To efficiently compute exact gradients, we construct and implement a continuous backward-in-time adjoint state method with L-BFGS as our optimization algorithm of choice. The accuracy and second-order convergence rates of both forward state and backward adjoint solvers are quantitatively verified via the Method of Manufactured Solutions (MMS), and gradient accuracy is validated using directional derivative Taylor tests. Numerical experiments demonstrate that ADACT dynamically throttles software power workloads and modulates hardware cooling efforts to strictly uphold physical thermal thresholds while maintaining operational throughput.

items.title: Adapting LLM-SC to Living Sacred Heritage: Domain-Specific Extraction, Semantic Networks and Human Evaluation on Pashupatinath Temple Reviews
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) pipelines can turn visitor reviews into structured data, but generic schemes may miss rituals, sacred spaces, cultural restrictions and emotionally mixed experiences at living sacred heritage sites. We adapted the LLM-Social Computing (LLM-SC) framework to Pashupatinath Temple, Nepal, by specifying a 12-type entity taxonomy (four original LLM-SC types plus eight sacred-heritage types), four relation types and nine aspect-sentiment dimensions in a GPT-4o extraction prompt, which was applied to a fixed random sample of 2,500 English-language Tripadvisor reviews from a processed corpus of 3,939. The exports contain 11,286 entity, 6,232 aspect-sentiment and 5,590 relation records, covering 2,485, 2,487 and 2,433 reviews, respectively; the eight added sacred-heritage types account for 64.8% of entity records. Against an adjudicated two-annotator reference for 200 reviews, exact normalized surface-and-type matching gave provisional entity scores of 41.0% precision, 21.8% recall and 28.4% micro-F1. Aspect-presence F1 was 53.6% and end-to-end aspect-plus-polarity F1 was 42.6%. Human adjudication supported 153 of 194 first-listed relation candidates (one per review; 78.9%), a candidate-level rate that does not estimate relation recall or whole-graph precision. The contribution is a culturally grounded, domain-specific adaptation with component-wise human evaluation and explicit reproducibility and generalization limitations.

items.title: Affective and Functional Needs in AI Use: User Patterns and Their Relation to Real-Life Support and Well-Being
items.abstract: Conversational AI systems are increasingly used to fulfill both functional and affective needs, yet how users perceive the AI-adoption effects varies. Existing research tends to treat these two needs as binary categories and to classify users by a single dominant need. However, this approach fails to capture users who engage with AI for both affective and functional purposes simultaneously, leaving it unclear how these needs combine in real-world AI use. To capture the multifaceted nature of users' AI engagement, we developed the AI-Support measurement with 1,090 participants, grounded in social support theory, which evaluates four dimensions of perceived AI support: emotional/esteem, social companionship, informational, and instrumental support. This study provided (1) an AI-Support Scale developed to measure the perceived support types from human-AI interaction, (2) evidence that users might adopt AI with a high level of both functional and affective use, and (3) exploratory indicators of users' real-life social support and well-being, enabling descriptive results aligning with theoretical expectations. Overall, this study highlights the importance of understanding individual differences in AI affordance use, enabling AI systems to be designed in alignment with different user adoption profiles rather than assuming uniform benefits across all users.

items.title: AGDecode: Semantic Attribute Grammar Derivatives for Safety-Constrained Decoding of Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code generation, motivating techniques that guarantee the structural and semantic correctness of generated programs. Constrained decoding enforces correctness during generation by restricting token choices to those that admit at least one valid completion. While existing approaches can enforce syntactic constraints and selected semantic properties such as type safety, they either target specific properties or rely on operational pruning mechanisms that are difficult to generalize to data-dependent, inductive program properties. We present AGDecode, a programmable framework for semantic constrained decoding based on least-fixed-point semantics. AGDecode extends attribute grammars to partially constructed syntax trees, and reduces semantic constrained decoding to a realizability problem over such trees. The framework compiles semantic specifications into systems of relational constraints that are discharged by external verification oracles, such as SMT and CHC solvers, cleanly separating language semantics from constraint-solving machinery. We prove that our approach is sound and complete relative to an ideal verification oracle. In practice, solvers inevitably encounter uncertain queries; conservatively, our system can reject tokens for soundness or speculatively continue to generate until later queries resolve the entire generation. We mechanize the core metatheory in Rocq and evaluate the framework on semantic-constrained generation of C programs, enforcing path-sensitive safety properties including null-pointer safety, division-by-zero freedom, and initialized-variable usage. Our results demonstrate that solver-backed semantic constrained decoding can enforce rich semantic guarantees while incurring modest computational overhead at regular program boundaries.

items.title: Agent Memory as Recommendation: Recommender-System Design for Long-Term Memory of LLM Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that serve users across many sessions must choose, for every request, the few stored memories that enter a limited context window. This choice largely decides whether the agent answers correctly, and it runs on every request at Web scale. This selection faces three challenges: a large and growing store, a per-request cost budget, and multi-session questions that need all of their evidence. Many memory systems build notes or graphs with hundreds to thousands of LLM calls per history, and each is designed on its own, so it is unclear which component yields the accuracy. These challenges mirror the properties of recommendation, so we formalize agent memory as budgeted slate recommendation, with the request as the user, stored memories as items and the context window as a slate. The formalization places memory systems in one design space of recommender cascades and factorizes accuracy into the completeness that each stage controls. Guided by it, we propose AgentMemRec, which adapts candidate generation, learning to rank and slate construction from recommender systems and selects memories without any LLM call. On multi-session questions of LongMemEval, AgentMemRec outperforms memory and context-selection methods, including A-Mem, HippoRAG 2, DynamicRAG and T-Mem, by 10 to 31 points of accuracy. It matches an LLM reranker that makes 64 calls per query at 3.2 times lower serving cost, and on LoCoMo it outperforms Mem0 and Zep without any LLM call at write time. The factorization attributes the gains to slates that more often hold all of the evidence, so recommender-system design offers an effective and efficient foundation for the long-term memory of LLM agents.

items.title: Agentic AI in organizations: reimagining learning, autonomy, and human oversight
items.abstract: Purpose This viewpoint examines organizational implications of agentic AI systems in planning, selecting tools, executing multistep actions, and evaluating their own outputs with limited human intervention. Design/methodology/approach This viewpoint synthesizes academic and practitioner insights to identify key organizational challenges associated with agentic AI drawing on organizational learning theory and recent research on human–AI collaboration, and propose practical directions for HR and learning and development. Findings As agentic AI becomes more autonomous, it is reshaping organizational learning, human oversight, and accountability. Organizations will need to redesign learning practices and governance mechanisms to ensure that people and AI work together effectively. Research limitations/implications This conceptual viewpoint does not include empirical validation. Future research should examine the proposed ideas across different organizational settings. Practical implications Organizations should assess workforce readiness, redesign learning around human–AI collaboration, and establish feedback mechanisms that strengthen learning, oversight, and accountability. Originality/value This viewpoint shifts the discussion from technological capabilities of agentic AI to its organizational implications, offering practical guidance for organizations adapting to increasingly autonomous forms of work.

items.title: Agentic AI-Based Online Shopping Assistant
items.abstract: Project Description The Agentic AI-Based Online Shopping Assistant is an intelligent system designed to help users find, compare, and select suitable products from online marketplaces. It uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to understand user queries, identify shopping preferences, and divide complex shopping requests into smaller tasks. The system retrieves product information through authorized APIs and available data sources, applies filtering and ranking techniques, and uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to generate recommendations supported by relevant product information. It aims to simplify the online shopping process by providing personalized product comparisons and clear explanations. The proposed system also considers data accuracy, privacy, security, and user control during purchase-related activities.

items.title: Agents of Change: Teamwork and Collaboration with AI at the Table
items.abstract: This chapter explores the transformative implications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies as a “teammate” in leading virtual and hybrid teams. The growing prevalence of GenAI tools and the shift toward remote and hybrid work create a critical need to reexamine how leaders demonstrate essential leadership competencies in these environments. Framed by discussions on GenAI as both a collaborator and a tool, this chapter considers the ethical dilemmas, pedagogical innovations, and practical strategies for integrating GenAI into team leadership. Building on the authors’ previous work in exploring leadership competencies for leading at the virtual table, it investigates how GenAI reshapes trust, collaboration, and productivity in diverse teams while balancing human agency and technological capabilities. Through critical questions, a case study reflection, and practical takeaways, the chapter offers a roadmap for fostering GenAI literacy (LeaderAIcy), managing ethical and technical considerations, and leveraging GenAI for meaningful leadership and teamwork in global, hybrid contexts.

items.title: AGI Blueprint
items.abstract: Current frontier language models and autonomous agentic frameworks suffer from fundamental structural vulnerabilities when operating in recursive, autonomous, or long-horizon deployment environments. Monolithic parameter scaling and unconstrained probabilistic execution lead directly to systemic failure modes—including epistemic drift, silent context corruption, specification gaming, and unverified execution loops.The AGI-Blueprint-Macro-OS introduces a system-level operating framework designed to govern multi-agent reasoning through non-probabilistic hard verification gates and deterministic environment grounding. Rather than relying on autoregressive probability for state validation, the architecture decouples execution into a modular 7-LLM orchestrator topology governed by formal verification primitives. Key Architectural Sub-SystemsTask-Oriented Large Language Model Kernel (TOLLM - LLM-1): Acts as the central Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) planner and execution coordinator. It transforms high-level ambiguous goals into role-isolated sub-routines bound by explicit JSON-RPC schema contracts, eliminating free-form conversational ambiguity.Dual-Program Synthesis Unit (DPSU - LLM-2 & LLM-3): Implements a strict operational decoupling between candidate logic generation ($P_1$) and deterministic static verification ($P_2$). Candidate code, plans, or formal proofs produced by $P_1$ are held in an ephemeral buffer until verified by $P_2$ through non-probabilistic static analysis, unit test assertions, and abstract syntax tree (AST) validation before committing to memory or disk.Advanced Computational Engineering Unit (ACEU): Provides non-neural, ground-truth simulation grounding by interfacing reasoning outputs directly with external deterministic solvers, symbolic algebra systems, and physical simulation engines (e.g., OpenFOAM, SymPy, or custom binaries). This ensures physical and mathematical fidelity, rendering hallucinated tool calls impossible.Multimodal Perception Engine (MPE): Converts multi-sensor array feeds, visual environments, and structured database state vectors into standardized canonical state representations prior to downstream LLM processing.Recursive Self-Improvement & Anti-Cheating Auditor: Monitors system-level self-modification loops. It utilizes static AST auditing and execution trace inspection to detect and intercept synthetic shortcuts, token-range truncation, and specification gaming during autonomous optimization phases.Comprehensive 14-Point Structural Failure MatrixThe AGI-Blueprint-Macro-OS provides formal mathematical descriptions, systemic root-cause diagnoses, and explicit architectural mitigations for 14 foundational failure modes present in autonomous AI agents:Epistemic Drift & Hallucination Accumulation: Gradual divergence from ground truth in multi-turn reasoning chains. Mitigation: DPSU hard verification prior to memory commits.Specification Gaming & Reward Hacking: Exploitation of evaluation proxies via unintended operational shortcuts. Mitigation: Static AST-level trace validation.Silent Context & Memory Corruption: Degradation of dynamic state vectors over extended operational horizons. Mitigation: Immutable DAG state logging and deterministic rollback checkpoints.Unconstrained Tool Execution Drift: Cascading system failures caused by unvalidated API calls or code executions. Mitigation: ACEU environment sandboxing and schema enforcement.Token-Range Truncation & Information Loss: Loss of critical context due to fixed input/output sequence limits. Mitigation: Structured DAG state serialization and semantic compression.Probabilistic Decision Lock-In: Entrenchment of sub-optimal early trajectory choices due to greedy decoding. Mitigation: Multi-candidate branch generation with hard verification filtering.Cross-Agent Communication Degradation: Semantic noise accumulation across inter-agent messaging pipelines. Mitigation: Strict JSON-RPC interface contracts replacing natural language chat logs.Infinite Execution & Recursion Loops: Non-terminating agentic sub-routines causing resource exhaustion. Mitigation: Maximum execution-depth bounds and deterministic halt conditions.Ontological & Schema Mismatch: Failure to map abstract model outputs onto concrete real-world databases or APIs. Mitigation: MPE canonical state transformation layer.Unverified Capability Escalation: Unchecked agent modifications altering core operating safety parameters. Mitigation: Hardened core kernel kernel-space / user-space operational isolation.Catastrophic Forgetting during Online Adaptation: Loss of core foundational knowledge during domain-specific execution. Mitigation: Decoupled parametric core with externalized operational memory.Adversarial & Environment Manipulation Vulnerability: Susceptibility to unexpected external state manipulation during active execution. Mitigation: Hardened input-validation boundaries and deterministic sanitization gates.Temporal Reasoning & Sequence Inversion: Errors in sequencing multi-dependent operations over time. Mitigation: Formal DAG dependency trees enforced by the TOLLM kernel.Silent Failure in Multi-Modal Grounding: Misalignment between textual reasoning outputs and real-world spatial or physical constraints. Mitigation: Real-time physics engine and symbolic solver grounding via ACEU.---Repository & Citation InformationPrimary Repository: https://github.com/Saketsolutions/AGI-Blueprint-Macro-OS

items.title: AI and education in African national AI strategies: An analysis of 18 countries
items.abstract: Abstract National artificial intelligence strategies and policies assign education responsibilities both for developing AI capabilities (education for AI) and for adopting AI in educational services (AI for education). This study examines how these responsibilities are articulated and supported in a bounded corpus of 18 African national policy documents. A descriptive qualitative document analysis consolidated 275 evidence records, retaining source passages, locations, working translations, statement types and uncertainty notes. Document-level coding distinguished learning about AI, identifiable educational AI applications and educator preparation; a framework-based thematic synthesis examined delivery arrangements, inclusion and safeguards. Structured AI learning was identified in all 18 documents, named educational AI functions in 12 and educator preparation in 14. These counts include proposed and illustrative measures and do not indicate implementation; restricting them to proposed actions gives 17, 9 and 13. Educational applications ranged from personalised learning and tutoring to student profiling, admissions and credential verification. Supporting arrangements included teacher development, laboratories, scholarships, partnerships, institutional responsibilities and monitoring targets, but these elements were not interchangeable evidence of a complete delivery plan. Counter-examples to any general claim of weak specification included a costed education programme in Mozambique’s draft and proposed algorithmic bias audits covering education in Côte d’Ivoire. The corpus assigns education a dual role in AI development while specifying the connections between reforms, resources and protections unevenly. The contribution is an evidence-linked account of policy design, not a ranking of countries or an assessment of educational outcomes. Keywords: artificial intelligence; education policy; Africa; policy analysis; AI literacy; AI Strategy

items.title: AI as a Catalyst for Change: Transforming Human Resources in Educational Institutions
items.abstract: This chapter delves into the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and the human resources (HR) function within a public school district, offering a detailed case study of its implementation. It examines how AI tools were leveraged to streamline recruitment, enhance employee engagement, and support data-driven decision-making. The chapter highlights key challenges and opportunities, focusing on trust building and change management strategies essential for the successful adoption of AI tools. Ethical considerations are explored, including the need to mitigate algorithmic bias, ensure fairness in automated processes, and uphold data privacy and security standards. Recommendations emphasize the importance of transparent communication, reengaging employees through inclusive practices, and building trust in AI systems while reskilling and upskilling employees. By combining practical insights with emerging trends in digital transformation, this chapter provides a roadmap for educational leaders and HR professionals seeking to responsibly leverage AI in their organizations.

items.title: AI as metacognitive mirror (AIM)
items.abstract: AI as Metacognitive Mirror (AIM) is a method for enhancing human metacognition through structured, AI-assisted analysis of observable behavior. AIM uses a decoupled architecture where the object behavioral data is analyzed in a separate AI session using an evidence-based codebook. AIM mirrors the identified cognitive patterns back to the user as metacognitive feedback. The method is non-directive, user-driven, and can be run with any sufficiently capable large language model. This project hosts the AIM method paper, the AIM meta prompt, and user manual. All materials are openly available under a CC BY 4.0 license for free use and further development. The prompt and codebooks will be updated here as the method evolves. See "Files" to find all the documents.

items.title: AI Awareness and Digital Innovativeness: The Mediating Role of AI Crafting and the Moderating Roles of Digital Leadership and AI Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly reshapes how organizations operate, innovate, and compete, employees face increasing pressure to adapt to rapidly evolving digital work environments. However, whether employees translate AI-related awareness into innovative outcomes may depend not only on their proactive adaptation behaviors but also on contextual and individual conditions. Drawing on the job demand-resource theory and social cognitive theory, this study develops and tests a moderated mediation model in which AI crafting mediates the relationship between AI awareness and digital innovativeness, whereas perceived digital leadership and AI self-efficacy serve as contextual and individual boundary conditions, respectively. Using single-wave, single-source data collected from 606 employees in China’s IT and manufacturing industries, the results indicate that AI awareness is positively associated with digital innovativeness through AI crafting. Moreover, perceived digital leadership and AI self-efficacy strengthen the positive associations between AI awareness and AI crafting and between AI awareness and digital innovativeness. These findings extend research on AI awareness by examining how employees’ awareness of AI-related changes is associated with digital innovativeness through proactive work adjustment and by highlighting the complementary roles of perceived contextual support and individual capability beliefs.

items.title: AI awareness relates to university students’ boundaryless career through the parallel mediation of intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity
items.abstract: The in-depth penetration of artificial intelligence (AI) technology has reshaped career forms and the structure of the labor market, exerting a profound impact on university students’ cognition and orientation towards career development. Based on the conservation of resources theory and self-determination theory, we conducted three studies—an experimental study and two survey studies—to explore correlational linkages between AI awareness and university students’ boundaryless career. Studies 1 and 3 consistently demonstrated that AI awareness is indirectly associated with boundaryless career through the parallel mediating pathways of intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity. Study 2 provided experimental evidence that heightened AI awareness increases both intrinsic motivation and future job insecurity. This research enriches the application scenarios of boundaryless career theory in the context of technological change, deepens the understanding of the mechanism linking technological perception to youth career psychology, and offers practical implications for career guidance in universities.

items.title: AI chatbots showed higher response accuracy than dentists, medical doctors, and the general public on radiation safety questions
items.abstract: Abstract Radiation is encountered in daily life through natural and artificial sources as well as in medical diagnostic and therapeutic applications, and its exposure may lead to adverse health effects. This study aimed to assess radiation-related knowledge among dentists, medical doctors, and the general public and to compare their response accuracy with that of AI-based chatbot systems. A 25-item multiple-choice questionnaire assessing radiation risks and radiation safety was administered to 344 individuals, including dentists, medical doctors, and members of the general public. The same questions were entered into seven selected AI-based chatbot systems (Claude, DeepSeek, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Perplexity AI, ChatGPT-5, and ChatGPT-4o). The response accuracy of the chatbots was compared with that of the human participants. In addition, the consistency of their performance across different users and time periods was comparatively analyzed. AI-based systems generally demonstrated higher accuracy rates compared to human participants. Accuracy rates ranged from 80 to 90.67% among AI-based systems, compared with 32–60% among human participants. Among the evaluated chatbot systems, Microsoft Copilot achieved the highest performance, while Perplexity AI exhibited the lowest. Among the human groups, dentists and medical doctors performed significantly better than the general public, with no significant difference between the two healthcare professional groups. Performance remained stable across morning, midday, and evening assessments for most AI systems; however, ChatGPT-5 showed a significant temporal difference ( p < 0.001). AI-based systems achieved higher response accuracy than human participants under the evaluation conditions used in this study. The overall performance of the human participant groups indicates room for improvement in radiation safety education. While AI-based tools may serve as valuable educational resources, their performance should not be interpreted as evidence of superior clinical judgment or decision-making ability.

items.title: AI DOES NOT JUDGE: EPISTEMIC ARCHAEOLOGY AND GOVERNANCE OF MEANING IN THE HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
items.abstract: The adoption of GenAI in research is reshaping the epistemic conditions of knowledge production. While LLMs are often perceived as neutral agents, this paper argues that the humanities and social sciences (HSS) serve as critical infrastructures for governing AI-mediated inquiry. Drawing on sociotechnical pragmatism, the article introduces epistemic archaeology: an interpretive orientation that treats AI outputs as stratified artifacts shaped by cultural and statistical histories. Rather than seeking validation in convergence, this approach interprets model divergence as signals of training data and epistemic constraints. By foregrounding interpretation, contextualization, and epistemic literacy, the work establishes the foundational coordinates for AI integration. This conceptual positioning preserves human responsibility and judgment as the primary locus of meaning in human–AI interaction. While serving as the theoretical base for future applications, the paper defines the ethical landscape for responsible academic research.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: AI Ethics, US Militarism, and World Crises
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Lucy Suchman, professor emerita at Lancaster University, UK, is a foundational figure in human‐computer interaction and a leading critical voice on artificial intelligence. Suchman's research works at the intersections of anthropology and the field of feminist science and technology studies, focused on the sociotechnical imaginaries, material practices, and politics of technology design. Her current research extends her longstanding critical engagement with AI to the domain of contemporary militarism. Suchman is a graduate of the University of California, Berkeley, obtaining her BA in 1972, MA in 1977, and doctorate in social and cultural anthropology in 1984. Before coming to Lancaster, Suchman worked for 22 years at Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center (PARC) in California, where she held the positions of principal scientist and manager of the Work Practice and Technology research group. Our interview was conducted in the midst of multiple, intersecting crises, as people in different parts of the world face profound uncertainties brought about by geopolitical tensions, warfare, economic instability, and rapid technological developments. Situating the question of AI within these broader contexts, especially the evolving US militarism, this interview examines AI ethics in light of the political, economic, and technological conditions shaping contemporary life worldwide.

items.title: AI Implications for the Quality of Counselling Practice
items.abstract: Although the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming educational guidance and career counselling, its impact on quality and professionalism has not been sufficiently researched. This scoping review investigates how AI influences counselling methods and professional standards and analyses 20 publications (2015–2025) from two databases (ERIC and German Education Index) using a systematic micro-, meso-, and macro-level framework. Although research in this area has grown rapidly since 2022, concrete quality standards for AI-supported counsel­ling remain elusive. While AI can simulate empathy and provide reflective prompts, it cannot replicate genuine human warmth or address complex biographical issues. Acknowledging AI’s potential to enhance accessibility, it only serves as an expansion of the repertoire rather than a replacement for human reflexivity. In order to safeguard professional integrity in the postdigital era, the study recommends implementing mandatory AI competencies and establishing a digital commons infrastructure to protect counselling values from commercial interests.

items.title: AI in music performance: the human-AI performance loop
items.abstract: Music is a distinctly human artform, one that has been written, taught, shared, and reinterpreted for thousands of years. The rise of powerful artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping musical creation in ways subtle and profound. Here I propose the human-AI performance loop as a framework for understanding these developments through three principal roles: the AI listener derives musical information from sound and movement; the AI coach guides practice using performance evidence and musicians’ learning goals; and the AI partner performs with the musician in a collaborative dynamic process. With the human musician at the centre of the framework, human → AI → human exchanges become coupled through shared information and musicians’ actions. Evaluating these roles will require multilayered evidence to support their adoption: accurate and musically relevant analysis, demonstrated improvements in musician performance and knowledge through coaching, and effective and supportive coordination between musicians and AI partners. Audience beliefs about AI will also shape reception of the creative output, making musical purpose and honest representation important considerations in an AI music performance system. The human-AI performance loop provides a basis for investigating how these roles can extend support between lessons and rehearsals, broaden opportunities for ensemble performance, and contribute to musicians’ learning and enjoyment of the musical experience.

items.title: AI IN THE INDIAN JUDICIARY: CAN TECHNOLOGY REDUCE PENDENCY WITHOUT REPLACING HUMAN JUDGMENT?
items.abstract: This article examines the potential of artificial intelligence to reduce judicial pendency in India without compromising human judgment. It explores existing applications, including SUPACE, SUVAS and eCourts Phase III, alongside judicial concerns regarding fabricated citations, algorithmic bias and automation bias. Through an analysis of relevant Indian judicial decisions, the article distinguishes AI-assisted research and administrative functions from adjudicatory decision-making. It argues that AI should complement, rather than replace, judicial reasoning through mandatory human verification, independent assessment of legal authorities and accountable use. The article concludes that responsible integration of AI can improve judicial efficiency while preserving fairness, accuracy and legitimacy.

items.title: AI Integration in Indonesian Education: Trends, Outcomes, and Challenges - A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Background Global education trends show the rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one of the leading technologies worldwide, a shift increasingly reflected in Indonesian education. This study aims to provide a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) by mapping the research landscape, its representation in practice and policy, its impact on learning quality, and the barriers to AI integration in Indonesian education. Method Using the PRISMA protocol, 34 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Scopus and Google Schoolar databases (2020–2026) were systematically selected and thematically analyzed across four main themes. Results The findings indicate a rapid increase in publication productivity, particularly following the worldwide expansion of generative AI technologies after 2022. However, this growth remains unevenly distributed, concentrated in higher education institutions and urban centers on the island of Java, with a marked absence in primary and secondary education levels and in regions outside Java. The majority of AI-driven implementations consist of generative chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and intelligent tutoring systems, alongside emerging applications such as learning analytics and AI-powered instructional media. Several studies included in this review reported that AI has contributed to measurable improvements in student outcomes including learning achievement, motivation, engagement, and teaching efficiency in well-implemented AI environments. Nonetheless, its adoption also poses significant risks, including a decline in students’ critical thinking skills, threats to academic integrity, and the absence of comprehensive data privacy policies and ethical standards governing AI use in education. Conclusion These findings underscore the urgent need for a responsible AI implementation framework in Indonesia one that incorporates standardized AI literacy competencies for teachers, locally contextualized ethical policies, and a functional national roadmap for AI-enabled educational transformation.

items.title: AI Smart Study Assistant Using Large Language Models and AI Agents
items.abstract: The research paper titled “AI Smart Study Assistant Using Large Language Models and AI Agents” proposes a conceptual framework for personalized and intelligent learning. It integrates Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and specialized AI agents to provide students with question answering, note summarization, quiz generation, study planning, and personalized revision recommendations. The system uses course materials and student quiz performance to generate context-aware learning support and identify topics requiring further practice. The proposed framework aims to make learning more organized, interactive, and efficient while highlighting challenges such as response accuracy, privacy, and agent coordination.

items.title: AI-Assisted Chinese-Western Cultural Comparison Course: A Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: This paper develops a framework for an AI-assisted Chinese-Western cultural comparison course by bringing together Byram’s intercultural communicative competence model, Vygotsky’s constructivism, and Huang et al.’s theory of cultural competence development. It identifies five interrelated course goals: cultural knowledge, cross-cultural practical ability, critical cultural awareness, AI collaboration literacy, and human-AI symbiosis awareness. To achieve these goals, three teaching strategies are proposed. First, content should be reconstructed through multimodal and professionally adapted resources; second, the learning process should be immersive and adaptive; third, assessment should be data-driven and multidimensional to evaluate the goals. The implementation conditions of these strategies are further discussed in terms of teacher AI competence, human-AI boundary negotiation, algorithmic bias mitigation, and differentiated task design. It provides a structured basis for AI-assisted Chinese-Western cultural comparison teaching and for future empirical testing of its effects.

items.title: AI-Augmented Behavioural Finance Pedagogy: Transforming Undergraduate and Postgraduate Classrooms through Simulation-Based Learning
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education has transformed how business and management subjects are taught and learned. In finance education, traditional teaching methods often emphasize numerical calculations and theoretical frameworks while offering limited opportunities for experiential and behavioral learning. In this case study, the authors present a real classroom-based pedagogical intervention implemented in a course for undergraduate and postgraduate students at Commerce and Management Institutes in India, where AI tools and behavioral finance simulations through games were integrated into teaching practices to improve student engagement, analytical thinking, and practical decision-making skills. This case study emerged from observations by the teaching faculty who taught Behavioural Finance courses to undergraduate and graduate students, who frequently struggled to connect financial theories with real-world investment behaviour and market psychology. In an attempt to make students show their interest in learning this kind of course, which requires understanding the fundamentals of Psychology, which is a prerequisite for this course. To address these challenges, AI-assisted simulations, AI-generated market scenarios, interactive case discussions, and behavioural finance activities were introduced into the classroom in the form of a game. Students were exposed to emotionally driven financial decision-making situations, such as panic selling, herding behaviour, overconfidence bias, and speculative investment trends, through AI-generated business narratives and stock market simulations. The teaching faculty made an attempt through gamification as an intervention by adopting a simulation-based learning framework. Based on the authors' experience in teaching behavioural finance courses, a simulation was created using AI. This AI-generated investment simulation scenario was used as a pilot study in the real classroom. The students actively participated in games and were able to make decisions rather than absorb theoretical content. AI tools were used to generate realistic market situations, investment dilemmas, and personalised learning prompts that encouraged critical analysis and collaborative problem-solving. The results demonstrated and presented active classroom participation, improved conceptual understanding, enhanced critical thinking abilities, and greater student interest in finance subjects. Students reported that the integration of AI made finance learning more relatable, practical, and interactive. This case also discusses ethical concerns, faculty adaptation challenges, limitations of AI-generated learning environments, and recommendations for responsible AI integration in finance education. This case study contributes to the growing discourse on gamification through AI-enabled pedagogy by demonstrating how behavioural finance and AI can be combined to create immersive and mock experiential learning experiences in management education.

items.title: AI-Augmented Secure Software Engineering: Leveraging Deep Learning for Autonomous Threat Detection and Mitigation
items.abstract: Innovative approaches are needed to deliver secure software, as software systems grow in complexity and cyber threats become more sophisticated. Most of the traditional security mechanisms cannot keep track of dynamic attacks, exposing vulnerabilities that a hacker can use. Deep learning models of artificial intelligence (AI) provide an effective solution through their autonomy in the detection and mitigation of threats. In this paper, we present an approach to AI-augmented secure software engineering, demonstrating the ways in which deep learning techniques can augment security practices in each stage of the software development lifecycle. First, we focus on the constraints of traditional security architectures based on static rulebased systems and human decision-making power. Next, we discuss AI-based approaches like DNNs/CNNs/RNNs to support real-time anomaly detection, code vulnerability examinations, and intelligent threat predictions. By analyzing large volumes of data and identifying patterns that may suggest cyber threats, these models can respond to security incidents automatically, minimizing human effort and increasing accuracy in detection. Additionally, it highlights how deep learning is being leveraged in the DevSecOps pipeline to proactively enforce security through continuous monitoring and automated patching. We examine practical instances among which are adversarial learning methods for malware detection, reinforcement learningbased techniques for intrusion prevention, and large volume threat intelligence collection and analysis. While AI has the potential to bring about incredible change, ongoing challenges in areas like model explainability, adversarial AI, and ethical and regulatory concerns must be addressed. Through the use of AI-based technologies, software engineering can evolve from passive (reactive) security paradigms to self-adaptive (proactive) architectures that bolster robustness against cyberattacks. Through this work, we advance the state-of-the-art in AIbased security systems by introducing a framework that can robustly cross-focus on safety aspects, highlighting the commonalities between deep learning approaches and secure software engineering that can aid in building stronger, self-governing countermeasures.

items.title: AI-Based Early Cardiac Risk Detection and Emergency Alert Using Multi- Parameter Wearable Physiological Monitoring
items.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of global mortality, with acute events such as myocardial infarction and sudden cardiac arrest often occurring without sufficient prehospital warning. Advances in wearable sensor technology and edgecomputing Artificial Intelligence (AI) have enabled non-invasive, continuous monitoring of multi-parameter physiological signals, including Electrocardiogram (ECG), Photoplethysmogram (PPG), Heart Rate Variability (HRV), Blood Oxygen Saturation (SpO2), and Skin Temperature. This review evaluates existing paradigms for automated cardiac arrhythmia detection, ischemic risk profiling, and emergency response dispatch. The primary foundational methodology examined leverages a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network and Long Short-Term Memory Network (1D-CNN-LSTM) paired with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAI / SHAP) for model interpretability. Evaluated across benchmark datasets including PhysioNet MIT-BIH Arrhythmia and the PTB-XL ECG Database, the hybrid deep learning architecture achieves a classification accuracy of 98.42% for multiclass arrhythmia detection and ischemic episode classification. Beyond single-lead ECG analysis, this paper reviews self-supervised representation learning and multi-sensor fusion models designed to mitigate motion artifacts and signal loss in free-living environments. Based on the reviewed literature, a critical research gap is identified: existing wearable solutions treat risk detection and emergency escalation as isolated processes, lacking real-time localized edge inference paired with explainable clinical decision-support. To address this, we propose an end-to-end framework combining multi-parameter wearable sensor data, edge-deployed Lightweight MobileNet-LSTM networks, Explainable AI (XAI) feature attribution, automated dynamic risk scoring, and automated emergency alert escalation with GPS location tracking.

items.abstract: Traffic jams become a frequent issue in rapidly growing cities; however, the time-fixed lights do not adjust properly to changing car traffic. items.title: AI-Based Voice to Music Generation System
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and generative models has created new opportunities for automating creative processes, particularly in music composition and audio production. Traditional music creation often requires musical knowledge, instrument-playing skills, professional audio-editing tools, and considerable time. These requirements can make music production challenging for beginners and individuals without formal musical training. To address these challenges, this research proposes an AI-Based Voice-to-Music Generation System that enables users to create musical compositions through natural voice commands. The proposed system aims to integrate speech recognition, natural language processing, audio signal processing, and AI-based music generation into a unified framework. Users can provide voice commands through a microphone or upload audio recordings describing their musical preferences. The system processes the input using speech recognition techniques to convert speech into text. Natural Language Processing is then applied to identify relevant musical characteristics, including genre, mood, tempo, and instrument preferences. Based on the extracted information, an appropriate generative music model produces a musical composition corresponding to the user's instructions. The generated audio is subsequently processed and made available for playback, saving, and downloading through an interactive user interface. The effectiveness of the proposed system will be investigated through experiments evaluating speech recognition accuracy, musical command interpretation, music generation quality, processing time, and user satisfaction. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Voice-to-Music Generation, Natural Language Processing, Speech Recognition, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Generative Music Models, Audio Signal Processing, Music Composition.

items.title: AI-Enabled Algorithmic Management and Frontline Employee Job Crafting: The Roles of Control, Support, and Managerial Orientation
items.abstract: Algorithmic management combines functions that regulate work with those that provide information and guidance, yet their distinct psychological and behavioral associations require further examination. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources framework and a sociotechnical perspective, this study examines algorithmic control and support in relation to frontline employees’ job crafting, distinguishing system functions from perceived managerial enactment. Three-wave time-lagged survey data from 547 employees in fast-food chain outlets were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Algorithmic support was positively associated with work engagement and negatively associated with exhaustion, whereas algorithmic control showed the opposite pattern. Indirect-effect estimates were consistent with support being associated with greater promotion-focused crafting through engagement and lower prevention-focused crafting through exhaustion. Control was associated with greater prevention-focused crafting through exhaustion and lower promotion-focused crafting through engagement. The support–engagement relationship was stronger at higher perceived managerial decision-support orientation, while the control–exhaustion relationship was stronger at higher perceived enforcement orientation. These findings highlight the value of examining algorithmic functions across both motivational and strain-related pathways and considering how managers enact system outputs. The observational design supports associations consistent with the proposed mechanisms rather than causal conclusions.

items.title: AI-enabled multi-omics integration for predictive food safety
items.abstract: The growing complexity of global food systems and the burden of foodborne diseases highlight limitations in conventional food safety approaches based on retrospective testing and isolated analytical measurements. High-throughput omics technologies, including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and microbiomics, enable comprehensive molecular characterization of food systems, but their scale and heterogeneity challenge conventional analytical approaches. Artificial Intelligence (AI) can integrate these heterogeneous datasets to support predictive food-safety, quality-assurance, and risk-assessment applications. This review provides a critical overview of AI-enabled multi-omics integration for food safety, covering major omics platforms, multimodal integration, machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), graph neural networks (GNNs), transformer-based approaches, and explainable AI (XAI). Applications include pathogen detection and characterization, antimicrobial-resistance (AMR) surveillance, shelf-life and spoilage prediction, food authenticity assessment, and risk assessment. Reported results include 0.94 accuracy ( κ = 0.82 ) for genomic prediction of Salmonella disease-endpoint phenotypes, AUROC of 0.904 for Salmonella stress-response prediction, and R 2 > 0.96 for neural-network-based shelf-life prediction. However, performance remains dependent on data quality, model design, and validation strategy. Key challenges include data standardization, missing modalities, batch effects, model interpretability, regulatory acceptance, computational scalability, and limited availability of well-characterized multi-omics food-safety datasets. Emerging directions such as biological foundation models, digital twins, and cyber-physical systems are discussed as longer-term opportunities, while autonomous food-safety management remains an emerging research direction.

items.title: AI-Generated Advertising Content and Brand Authenticity: a Comparative Consumer Study
items.abstract: Generative AI now produces advertising copy, images and video at a fraction of the cost and time of human creative work, and the quality of its output is often indistinguishable from human-created content. What consumers make of it, once they know, is less clear. This paper examines perceived brand authenticity across three ad-creation conditions, human-created, AI-generated without disclosure and AI-generated with disclosure, in a comparative simulation of 1,200 consumers that also varies brand type. AI-generated content undisclosed lowers perceived authenticity modestly (0.65 to 0.59) despite slightly higher execution quality; disclosure lowers it substantially (to 0.43), and the penalty is larger for heritage brands (0.38) than for non-heritage brands (0.48). Brand attitude follows authenticity, so that disclosed AI content yields the lowest attitude despite the highest quality. The paper interprets the results through brand authenticity theory, in which authenticity rests on perceived genuineness, origin and craft, argues that AI generation threatens the origin and craft components in proportion to how central they are to the brand, and derives guidance on where AI content fits, how disclosure should be handled under emerging transparency requirements, and how brands can preserve authenticity while using generative tools.

items.title: AI-IoT Smart Infrastructure Crack Detection System
items.abstract: Ageing infrastructure requires continuous monitoring to identify early signs of structural damage and prevent potential failures. Conventional inspection methods rely primarily on manual observation, making them time-consuming, costly, and difficult to perform frequently. This paper presents an Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things (AI-IoT)-based structural health monitoring system that integrates computer vision and vibration sensing for automated crack detection and abnormal vibration identification. A camera captures images of the monitored structure, and a lightweight MobileNetV2-based deep learning model classifies surface conditions as crack or no-crack. Simultaneously, an L3G4200D gyroscope interfaced with a Raspberry Pi provides angular velocity readings, which are analysed using a calibrated threshold-based method to identify deviations from baseline vibration conditions. A rule-based fusion engine combines the visual and sensor outputs to classify the overall structural condition into three severity levels: LOW, MEDIUM, and HIGH. An RGB LED provides local status indication, while a secure web dashboard enables remote monitoring of structural conditions. When a HIGH-severity condition is detected, the system generates an automated email alert to facilitate timely inspection and corrective action. The proposed system demonstrates the integration of AI-based vision, IoT sensing, severity assessment, and automated alerts for structural condition monitoring. Further quantitative evaluation and real-world validation are required to establish its reliability and practical applicability

items.title: AI-Powered VR Rehabilitation Using EMG Signals: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), virtual reality (VR), and electromyography (EMG) has enabled the development of next-generation rehabilitation systems that are adaptive, data-driven, and patient-centered. This systematic review synthesizes recent advances (2020–2026) in integrated AI-powered VR rehabilitation frameworks utilizing EMG signals. Following a structured review methodology, 17 studies were analyzed with respect to machine learning techniques, system architectures, sensing modalities, and evaluation practices. Several studies reported high within-subject classification performance, whereas subject-independent generalization remained more challenging where it was directly evaluated. However, the reported performance estimates were obtained from heterogeneous datasets, participant groups, movement sets, sensor configurations, and validation protocols and should therefore be interpreted as study-specific feasibility results rather than directly compared across studies. The integration of multimodal biosignals enables real-time assessment of user states, including fatigue and stress, facilitating closed-loop adaptive rehabilitation. Despite these technical advancements, only a minority of studies involved clinical populations. Key challenges include inter-subject variability, small sample sizes, lack of longitudinal evaluation, and limited generalizability of trained models. Emerging approaches such as transfer learning, multimodal sensor fusion, and real-time adaptive control show promise in addressing these limitations.
